sections.title: Scope, terms and status
sections.html:
How real SPHEREx exposures of a patch of sky become pictures in which motion is seen at once, how moving objects are found in them and how their spectra are measured. Every step is given with its parameters, the reason for the choice and the check that was made on real data.

358real Level 2 exposures of one field from the IRSA archive
3 passesAug 2025, Mar 2026, Aug 2026
102 channels0.75–5.0 µm, six detectors
6.15″SPHEREx pixel size
10.2″shift of the star in one year: 1.7 pixels
10.40″/yrmeasured from these frames; Gaia DR3: 10.39

The numbers above are the main test field, Barnard's Star. The same code was run on ε Indi B and on one square degree on the ecliptic (section “Test fields”).

Terms. The mission calls one detector's Level-2 file a spectral image; here it is an exposure. SPHEREx observes each sky position through six detectors (D1–D6) at once, in three pairs that see the same sky at the same time (D1/D4, D2/D5, D3/D6), so a count of exposures is a count of detector images, not of distinct pointings. A visit is a run of exposures of one detector taken minutes apart (typically four, two minutes apart). A pass is a cluster of visits separated from the next one by more than 60 days; the interface of the lab calls it a season. It is our own grouping, not one of the mission's numbered surveys. A super-frame is the stack of the exposures of one pass. A band is our own wavelength window with a plain name (Starlight, Water vapor, Methane and so on), not a mission band name.

Data. Every picture and number comes from a real archive query; nothing is simulated. A picture is made of the pixel values of the Level-2 files after background subtraction, stacking on a fine grid, a smoothing of 0.8 grid pixel, a brightness stretch and false color. A place without a measurement stays empty: a saturated core is white, a place that no exposure covers is flat blue-grey. Markers, path lines, speed rings and captions are drawn on top.

Code. The method is implemented in Python in this project. motion_pipeline/ holds the stacking, the searches and the spectra; it produced every video and number of the sections on super-frames, views, spectra and searches from exposures of the three test fields, on 9–11 November 2026. service/ is the sky service: the exposure index of the whole archive, the reads from the public copy of the archive and the catalog queries. The lab (the interactive screen of this application) is being moved onto the same algorithms; the table says, step by step, what the lab computes today.

sections.title: Data and provenance
sections.html:
DataSource and how it is read
SPHEREx Level-2 imagesNASA/IPAC IRSA, public S3 bucket nasa-irsa-spherex (QR2, QR3 and deep collections). The sky service reads only the pixels of the requested field by HTTP range requests.
Which exposures contain a positionOwn exposure index of the whole archive (12-vertex SIP footprints, HEALPix shards); until it is complete the IRSA SIA2 service is asked instead (source=sia). Both give the same list; the periods already indexed were reconciled against IRSA ObsCore counts per collection and period. The Index page shows its live state (151 periods, 1,607,473 files on 2026-11-11).
StarsGaia DR3 (G < 17.5, GAVO dr3lite), positions moved with proper motion; fainter stars are not circled.
Names, types, proper motionSIMBAD (CDS) through the service's resolver. Parallax for a callout must come from Gaia DR3, not from SIMBAD's basic entry (known inconsistency for RW Aur).
Archive epochAllWISE W2 (4.6 µm) atlas image, mid-epoch 2010, via IRSA IBE, on the same pixel grid.
Small bodiesJPL SBDB and Horizons, IMCCE SkyBoT (served by the service). The map draws a body's path from Horizons geocentric positions (SPHEREx is in low Earth orbit: the direction differs by about 5 pixels for a body at 0.3 au, by about a field only for a body closer than about 0.013 au, five lunar distances), and Open in lab loads a window of the visit nearest the path; the body may lie outside the 12′ field in other frames.
Cutouts for the pipelineThe runs of motion_pipeline/ on the test fields use the IRSA cutout of every exposure, which carries all extensions (image, flags, variance, zodiacal model, PSF): see Super-frames, step 1. When the IRSA query service does not answer, the exposure list is built from the public S3 copy by reading only the file headers.
Archive imagesDSS plate scans (STScI), 2MASS and WISE (IRSA Finder Chart), Pan-STARRS1 (STScI): see Time machine.
Catalog fluxes for the checks2MASS Point Source Catalog and AllWISE (IRSA TAP); filter curves from the SVO Filter Profile Service.

sections.title: Pixel values, units and flags
sections.html:
Pixel values are surface brightness in MJy/sr as stored in the Level-2 IMAGE extension. The zodiacal-light model is not subtracted from IMAGE (IRSA gives it separately in the ZODI extension), so the diffuse light left in an image includes the zodiacal light, which changes with the viewing geometry. The background is therefore removed per exposure, in one of two ways. The pipeline works on cutouts with all extensions: it subtracts ZODI and then the sigma-clipped median of what is left (Super-frames, step 2). The sky service reads IMAGE and the full FLAGS word of the box it needs and subtracts the sigma-clipped median of the box from each exposure; ZODI and VARIANCE are not read for the pictures (at 5′ the white frames with and without ZODI differ by 0.5 % of their noise). The old co-add of the lab, which is still used for the other views, takes the sky level of each exposure (sky_mjy_sr, the median of the cutout, which the halo of a bright star raises) and a pixel noise (sigma_mjy_sr) from the service and subtracts that level before any combination. Point spectra use a local background and do not depend on this choice. No flat-fielding, background modelling or PSF matching is done beyond what the SPHEREx pipeline did.

Flags in the lab. The service merges the named bits of the pipeline's flag word into four groups:

Service flag valuePipeline FLAGS names merged into itTreatment (BADFLAGS = 13)
1OVERFLOW, NONLINEAR, BLOOM (saturation, non-linear response, bloom)masked
2SOURCE (the pipeline’s own source mask)kept (not an error)
4TRANSIENT, PERSIST, OUTLIER, SNOWBALL, HALO, SATELLITE_HALO, CROSSTALK, STREAK, GHOST, GHOST_FPA, GHOST_EXTmasked
8SUR_ERROR, PHANTOM, REFERENCE, NONFUNC, DICHROIC, MISSING_DATA, HOT, COLD, PHANMISS, and every pixel outside the detector footprintmasked

The service reads the pipeline's flag word per pixel and merges its named bits into these four display groups (GROUPS in the service source). The bit numbers are read from each file's own header table (cards MP_<NAME> or MSKN/MSKM); a built-in table is used only if a file has none, and the service logs any mismatch. FULLSAMPLE is in no group and is ignored. The bits of the pipeline's own VARIANCE and ZODI extensions are not read.

Pixels that are NaN (outside an exposure's footprint) are treated as no data. A pixel with no usable value in a season and band is drawn flat blue-grey (no data), not black, so that “no coverage” cannot be mistaken for “no source”.

Flags in the pipeline. The pipeline uses the bits themselves. Bits 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 19 and 27 (dead, lost and outlier pixels) are always masked for the stacks of the fixed sky. Bits 0, 1, 2 and 17 (transient, overflow, processing error, residual charge) are masked only farther than 6 pixels from the target, because around a bright target they are set almost always and masking them everywhere would leave a hole where the star is. A saturated core (overflow bit or no value, within 4.5 pixels of the target) goes into no stack and is filled with nothing. Bit 19 (OUTLIER) is a special case: the SPHEREx pipeline sets it on the pixels of asteroids, so it is masked for the fixed sky and kept for the searches of moving objects (field near the ecliptic).

sections.title: Wavelength of a pixel
sections.html: An exposure measures one wavelength per sky position through a linear variable filter, and the wavelength changes slowly across the picture. The service supplies a 5 × 5 grid of the wavelength over each cutout (from the file's WCS-WAVE table with a bicubic spline between its nodes, including the spectral calibration v3.0 offset for D5 and D6; the service README documents a median difference to IRSA's own tool of +0.00003 µm on 123 ε Indi B measurements). We interpolate that grid bilinearly to every pixel. All wavelengths are in µm.

sections.title: Detectors, resolution and depth
sections.html:
SPHEREx has six H2RG detectors, D1–D3 in the short-wavelength arm and D4–D6 in the long one. Each carries a linear variable filter, so a pixel's wavelength depends on where it lies. The table gives the nominal wavelength coverage and spectral resolving power R = λ/Δλ of each detector from the mission's public description (Crill et al. 2020; Doré et al. 2014), and the single-frame 5σ point-source depth that the project's own checks derived (AB magnitude; not a stack and not a mission number). This application does not use these values for any image; the change test uses R to size its wavelength bins (section “Object card”).

sections.title: Bands: wavelength windows
sections.html:
A band is a set of wavelength windows. For each pixel, an exposure contributes to a band only if its wavelength at that pixel lies inside one of the windows (half-open, lower edge included). The windows below are our own working definitions of broad tracers, not line fluxes. Windows may overlap (the 3.2–3.5 µm methane window and the 3.2–3.4 µm dust window share exposures).

#BandWindowsWhat it traces
1Starlight0.75–1.10 µmOrdinary stars, continuum of cool stars
2Water vapor (H₂O)1.30–1.50 · 1.80–2.00 · 2.55–2.90 µmSteam in the atmospheres of cool stars and brown dwarfs
3Methane (CH₄)1.62–1.76 · 3.20–3.50 µmMethane in brown dwarfs and giant-planet atmospheres
4Water ice2.90–3.20 µmIce in comets, discs and dense clouds
5Dust (PAH)3.20–3.40 µmOrganic dust (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons)
6Carbon dioxide (CO₂)4.20–4.35 µmCO₂ gas and ice in comets and shells
7Carbon monoxide (CO)4.55–4.85 µmCold gas and discs

Limit. A band image shows continuum plus any feature: for stars it is dominated by the star's continuum. A feature (an absorption or an emission) can be claimed only from a continuum-subtracted map or a spectrum; band images alone never support a molecule claim. Continuum-subtracted maps are planned.

sections.title: Why the raw frames do not show motion
sections.html:
SPHEREx observes through a linear variable filter: each exposure sees the target at a different wavelength, at a different angle and on a different pixel grid. One pass collects about 120 frames over two to six weeks, then half a year of silence. If you step through the frames in order, the eye sees the blink of the spectrum and the jitter of the pixels, and the real shift — three steps of a third of a pixel against the noise — is lost.

All 358 frames in the order they were taken. Processing: background subtracted, frame rotated north up; pixels are not smoothed. The white squares at the center of the star are saturated pixels: the file has no value in their place. This is what the “slider” looks like. Next — what to do about it.

Second example: ε Indi B

369 frames of ε Indi B in the order they were taken. The object is not saturated, there are no white squares. The shift over 1.4 years is one pixel, and it is not visible in the raw movie either.

sections.title: Super-frames: from 358 exposures, three clean images
sections.html:
All the views below rest on one preparation step. It is done once per request, and every view is then computed from its output.

1. Find and download

# list of exposures covering the point (IRSA TAP, ADQL)
POST https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/TAP/sync
QUERY = SELECT a.uri, p.energy_bandpassname, p.time_bounds_lower
        FROM spherex.artifact a
        JOIN spherex.plane p ON a.planeid = p.planeid
        WHERE 1 = CONTAINS(POINT('ICRS', :ra, :dec), p.poly)
# cutout around the point (degrees)
GET https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/{uri}?center={ra},{dec}&size={deg}
  • A cutout is a FITS file with the extensions IMAGE (MJy/sr), FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI, WCS-WAVE and a PSF. In the QR2 release the PSF is stored as a PSF cube 101×101×121 (×10 finer than the pixel), in QR3 as an EPSF table of 21×21 zones, 33×33 each (×5). The code must understand both.
  • Each cutout weighs about 5 MB because of the PSF, even if the image is 70×70. Pictures do not need the PSF, the spectrum does; everything else is cached by obs_id.
  • The archive sometimes answers 503 “Server busy”, so a retry with a pause is needed. Five parallel streams work.

2. Clean up the frame

img  = IMAGE - ZODI
img -= sigma_clipped_median(img)            # 3 iterations at 3σ
lam, dlam = WCS(hdr, fobj=hdul, key='W').all_pix2world(x, y, 0)
t    = hdr['MJD-AVG'];  det = hdr['DETECTOR']
BAD_ALWAYS = bits 4,5,6,9,10,11,19,27       # dead, lost, outliers
BAD_FAR    = bits 0,1,2,17                  # transient, overflow, error, residual charge
sat  = (isnan(IMAGE) | flags & OVERFLOW) & r_target < 4.5px      # saturated core
mask = finite(img) & !sat & !(flags & BAD_ALWAYS) & !((flags & BAD_FAR) & r_target > 6px)

Flags 0–2 are set almost always around a bright target. If they are masked everywhere, the stack has a hole where the star is, so near the target they stay. The saturated core (bit 1 or NaN, 3–6 pixels in every frame) is not filled with anything: these pixels do not go into the stack.

3. Stack with super-resolution

The 6.15″ pixel is larger than the image of a star, and the frames of one pass are shifted relative to each other at random. If each frame is first interpolated and then averaged, everything blurs. Instead, each original pixel throws its value onto a grid four times finer, and the normalization is done over all frames at once.

S = 6.15 / 4            # 1.5375″ per grid pixel, north up
sig = 0.50 * 6.15 / S   # kernel sigma in grid pixels (0.30 in the offline pipeline, see below)
num = den = zeros(N, N)
for exp in stack:                       # frames of one pass and one detector
    u, v = sky_to_grid(exp.ra_pix, exp.dec_pix) + shift[exp]
    for (dx, dy) in window(-K..K), K = ceil(3*sig):
        x, y = round(u)+dx, round(v)+dy
        w = exp(-((x-u)**2 + (y-v)**2) / (2*sig**2)) * exp.weight
        num[y, x] += w * exp.img;   den[y, x] += w
stack = num / den

Field sizes in the lab. 2′, 5′, 10′, 20′ and 60′. Every field is built from all the exposures whose footprint overlaps it, not only those that contain its centre (the index is asked at a 3 × 3 grid of points over the field up to 20′ and a 5 × 5 grid above; a field with more than 800 exposures, such as R Draconis near the ecliptic pole, is thinned to 800, keeping every pass and detector). The grid step is 1.5375″ up to 20′ (N up to about 800) and 3.075″ at 60′ (N about 1170). From 10′ the background of every exposure also removes what depends on wavelength alone (the median in 40 wavelength bins: the helium airglow line at 1.083 µm is a stripe of +1.4 MJy/sr across D1), and above 12′ the per-visit test is not run.

The build does not hold the exposures. Pass by pass, every exposure is read once and its pixels are added to the sums (numerator and weight, before the smoothing) of its detector; then every exposure is read again (from the window cache on disk: no network) and tested against the other exposures of its pass and detector, which are those sums minus its own deposit (the leave-one-out test, smoothed only inside the footprint of the exposure); what a rejected pixel contributed is taken out of the sums at once, so the exposures that follow see the stack without it, and the pixels that stay go into the final sums of the detector, of the seven bands, of the saturated share and of the flag census. The sums are smoothed once, the pass is registered on pass 0 (field stars of the two white frames) by shifting the smoothed numerator and weight with a cubic spline (they are band-limited by the smoothing, so this equals depositing at the shifted positions), and the pass is written and dropped. Differences to the earlier build that kept every exposure in memory: the test is one pass with online updates instead of repeated rounds, the passes are registered on pass 0 instead of on their mean, and the census uses unregistered positions; on the test field the white frames agree to 10−4 MJy/sr. A field of 12′ or less keeps the per-visit test and reads and tests the exposures of one detector and pass together. Memory of the service for a 60′ field of 603 exposures: 1.1 GB at the peak (it was 3.5–5 GB for a 20′ field).

What the viewer receives. A quick frame first (white light, from 2 to 4 exposures per pass and detector). Then the picture part: spectral colour (red, green, blue, computed from the six detector stacks with the matrix of section “Spectral color”, in float16 with one validity plane) of every finished pass, rewritten after each pass: the lab shows the colour pendulum as soon as two passes are complete and says how many are (“colour for 2 of 3 passes complete”). The detector stacks (wall of detectors), the band stacks (wall of bands, a choice of bands) and the Difference maps are separate parts, fetched when their view is opened (all of them at once for a field of 10′ or less). Sizes of the Picture part at the three sizes of the test (3 passes): 0.9 MB at 5′, 14.8 MB at 20′, 33 MB at 60′, as sent (gzip) 0.6, 10.2 and 23 MB. Nothing is quantised: the values are float16 as before. Reading is limited by the link (13–15 MB/s): an exposure costs 1.2 MB at 5′, 4 MB at 20′ and 12 MB at 60′ (rows of 2040 pixels are read whole), so a cold 20′ field of 500 exposures takes about 2 minutes and a cold 60′ field of 600–700 exposures 10–12; the next pass is read while the current one is stacked, so that time is the network's.

  • Stacks are built separately for each pass and each detector (3×6 of them, 17–25 frames each). The “white” frame of a pass is the mean of the six detector stacks. This way all passes have the same wavelength composition, and nothing “breathes” during the blink. If some detector did not image the target in one of the passes (fewer than four exposures), it is left out of the white frame in every pass: white = nanmean(dets[:, CDET]), where CDET is the detectors present in all passes.
  • Passes are clusters of exposures separated by a gap of more than 60 days. The lab finds them with this rule for any field and cuts a pass at 90 days, so that a field observed without a break (near the ecliptic poles: R Draconis) still gives several frames; for the three test fields of the pipeline the same boundaries are written in target.py. A pass is our own grouping, not one of the mission's numbered surveys.
  • Before stacking, cosmic-ray hits are removed from each exposure: this is a separate step, step 5.
  • Registration: centroids of the field stars in each pass, the median shift is subtracted. The residual after this is 0.05″.
  • Saturation: along with the stack, the fraction of contributions from saturated pixels is accumulated, sat = Σw_sat / (Σw + Σw_sat). Where it is above 0.5, the point on the screen is white: “no measurement here”. No pixel value is made up. The brightest real value in the stacks is 1600 MJy/sr. The fraction is computed only over the detectors of the white frame. Otherwise a detector with three or four exposures declares a spot saturated because of one flagged pixel in one exposure, and white dots appear in the picture far from the stars (seen on ε Indi B, where D1 and D4 have three or four exposures per pass).
  • Display: s = asinh((x−lo)/soft) / asinh((hi−lo)/soft), lo = −0.05, hi = 400, soft = 0.4 MJy/sr, plus Gaussian smoothing of 0.8 grid pixels.
  • Kernel width in the application: 0.50 detector pixel. With 0.30, the offline value, the stack follows single detector pixels where the dithers cover the grid thinly, and the pattern differs from pass to pass: the difference of two passes on empty sky shows a lattice at the pixel pitch (rms 0.089 MJy/sr against a noise floor of 0.054). The lattice would blink in the pendulum. The rms of the difference is 0.067 at 0.40, 0.058 at 0.50 and 0.055 at 0.60, where nothing but noise is left; stars are broader by 7 %, 14 % and 22 % than at 0.30. The application uses 0.50. The numbers on this page that come from the offline run (0.30) are labelled as such.

4. Measure the target position

The core of Barnard's Star is saturated in every frame. The center is taken from the wings: a Moffat profile is fitted to the unsaturated pixels within a radius of 8 pixels with a robust loss function, the position is converted to sky coordinates through the frame WCS, and the median is taken over the pass. For faint targets an ordinary centroid is enough.

5. Cosmic-ray hits: how to recognize them

A charged particle flies through the detector and leaves charge in one or two pixels of one exposure. Some of these traces reach the Level 2 files without a flag. In the picture it is a bright dot that is present in one pass and absent in another. For a tool that looks for motion, this is a ready-made false candidate.

  • Present in one exposure, with nothing at that spot on the sky in the others. This is the main sign. A real source is visible in every exposure of the pass.
  • Small. Of 160 traces in the narrow cutouts, 137 occupy one pixel, 15 — two, 8 — three or more.
  • Sharper than a star. A star is blurred by the optics. In D4–D6 its central pixel is never more than 4–6 times brighter than the brightest of its four neighbors (computed from the PSF in the files). For half of the traces this ratio is above 8.
  • In D1–D3 one frame is not enough. There a star that lands at the center of a pixel gives it 62–70% of its light and itself looks like a single pixel: the ratio to the neighbor reaches 7–14. It can be told from a trace only by the first sign.
  • No flags. Pixels with the outlier and transient flags are removed by the mask of step 2. These traces passed it.
  • Any brightness. In the narrow cutouts the median is 0.8 MJy/sr above the background, the brightest is 29. In the 1° cutouts they reach 600 MJy/sr: that is several times brighter than the core of a 9th-magnitude star.
  • More frequent in the long-wavelength detectors. Of 195 rejected pixels: D4 — 35, D5 — 40, D6 — 117.

How to remove them

# first pass: stacks num, den over all exposures (step 3)
for exp in stack:                              # same pass, same detector
    num_e, den_e = splat(exp)                  # contribution of the exposure itself
    others = (num - num_e) / (den - den_e)     # the same sky WITHOUT it
    peak   = max_filter(others, 1 original pixel)
    sigma  = 1.4826 * MAD(exp.img[sky])        # background noise of the exposure
    val, o, pk = exp.img, others[at pixel], peak[at pixel]
    hit  = (val - max(o, 0) > 8*sigma) & (val > 5*max(pk, 0))   # brighter than what the others see
    hit |= (o - val > 8*sigma + 5*abs(o))                         # or a dip
    exp.mask[hit] = False
# the check repeats while it finds anything new; then the stacks are rebuilt without the rejected pixels
  • The pixel is not replaced with anything: it simply does not go into the sum. In its place the stack keeps the values of the other exposures.
  • Both conditions are needed. The “8σ” one alone threw out 400 thousand pixels in the 1° cutouts, mostly star cores: with a pixel this large, a star honestly gives different values in neighboring exposures. The condition “five times brighter than anything the others see nearby” removes that.
  • A source is never rejected as a hit. Where the stack of the other exposures is above 5 σ of this exposure's single-pixel noise, and the pixel is less than 20 times the others' peak, the pixel stays: the flux of a source changes with the wavelength of each exposure (the core of ε Indi B is up to ten times brighter in some D1 exposures than in others) and a hit on top of it does not stay that low. In empty sky nothing changes (the share of injected hits that are rejected: 0.65, 0.74, 0.81 for hits of 2, 10 and 50 MJy/sr on Barnard's Star fields before and after); a hit that lands on a star core of 3–80 MJy/sr is kept (of 50 MJy/sr: 38 % rejected before, 7 % after).
  • The comparison must be with the stack without the exposure itself. A bright trace raises the common stack by itself and passes the check. One such trace of 596 MJy/sr produced a false track of 4.3″/yr.
  • One round is not enough when two hits landed next to each other. At ε Indi B a hit of 7 MJy/sr remained as a red dot in the spectral-color picture: one pixel away from it, in another exposure, there was a hit of 113 MJy/sr. It raised the “others”, and the “five times brighter” condition did not fire. So the check repeats while it finds anything new: the second and third rounds added 40 pixels at ε Indi B (758 → 798) and one at Barnard's Star.
  • First subtract the background by wavelength. Otherwise the helium 1.083 µm band in D1 ends up among the outliers: with it the rejection took ten times more pixels.
  • Total: 195 pixels in the narrow cutouts; 23 thousand (0.02%) in the 1° cutouts, a median of 37 per exposure.
  • When a spectrum is measured, the rejection is its own, per single exposure: a pixel that departs from the PSF fit by more than 6σ does not take part; a spectrum point that falls out of line with its wavelength neighbors is discarded. Details are in the spectrum check.
  • The ready-made single-frame tool, L.A.Cosmic (astroscrappy), does not work here. We ran it on 36 exposures with six sets of settings. With the default settings it flags 42 thousand pixels per exposure in D1–D3, and 32 thousand of them are real stars: with a pixel this large it cannot tell a star from a trace. The best of the six sets finds half of the traces rejected by comparing exposures (46–56%) and still flags 150 to 1360 star pixels per exposure.
  • A risk for the task itself: an object that shifts by more than a pixel between exposures is also “present in one exposure, empty in the others.” So the rejected pixels are not lost: they are collected into a list (singles.py): 15,572 detections, 2169 of them star-like (there is light in the neighboring pixels). No three of them lie on one straight line with constant speed; on scrambled data such a search gives 0.1 chance triples.
  • Two known 18th-magnitude asteroids that crossed the field did not get into this list in any of the 46 exposures: their pixels are fainter than the 8σ threshold. The rejection did not erase them. But they are not in the super-frames either: at each place on the sky an asteroid is visible in one visit of four exposures out of twenty. How to measure them anyway is in the check on asteroids.
  • In the raw movie of the previous section the traces are left in: the pixels there are shown as they are.

6. Halos of bright stars

Around a bright star the stack has a halo with spikes and rings. Between passes the telescope is rotated differently, the spikes land in other places, and the search takes them for sources that appeared or moved. Two rules remove this.

# 1. which saturated zones are real
zones = connected(sat > 0.5)
real  = [z for z in zones if area(z) >= (6.15″ / grid step)**2]     # at least one SPHEREx pixel
# a saturated zone is one source at its center, however wide its flat top is
# 2. halo light: the stack without point sources
halo = gauss(minimum_filter(stack, 25″), 12″)
hl   = max(halo - median(halo), 0)
# a source is accepted only if it stands above the halo
keep = (sm - halo > 8 * noise) and (sm - halo > 3 * hl)
  • A hard radius mask does not work. In the ε Indi field on the 1° grid, ε Indi B itself lies in the halo of ε Indi A, and the mask erased it. The contrast rule keeps it: it is hundreds of times brighter than the halo at its position.
  • ε Indi field, 1°: without the rules 5 tracks, 3 of them false (3.4, 84.7 and 105″/yr, all in the halo); with the rules the two real ones remain. Unmatched sources: 468 without the rules, 342 with them.
  • Barnard's Star field, 1°: one track in both cases; unmatched sources: 360 without the rules, 309 with them. The field is dense, with many bright stars, but their halos are small: the threshold is raised over 1.4% of the area, versus 6.6% for ε Indi.
  • Code: halomask.py; the rules are applied in detect.py.

What it looks like

ε Indi field. Yellow fills the area where the halo sets the threshold. The red crosses are the three false tracks that the search found without the rules.

Barnard's Star field. More bright stars, smaller zones.

7. Streaks and blotches of a single visit

For ε Indi B, in some of the D5 and D6 exposures a faint streak extends from the object: 0.1–0.2 MJy/sr, 3–4 pixels wide, more than 25 long. It runs along the detector row, roughly toward the bright ε Indi A. In October 2025 it is in 5 of 12 D6 visits, in September 2026 in 3 of 13 D5 visits. There are no flags on these pixels. In spectral color long wavelengths are red, so in the spectral-color picture the streak looks like red blotches around the object.

  • Cosmic-ray rejection does not see it. In a single pixel it is at the 2–4σ level and repeats in all exposures of the visit.
  • Signature. Present in one visit, while in most visits of the same pass and detector this place on the sky is empty. It covers tens of pixels.
  • The cause is not established. It may be scattered light from ε Indi A or a processing artifact; the Level 2 files do not tell which.
  • Barnard's Star has almost none of this: two blotches in two exposures.

Detector D6, October 2025. Left: the stack before the check; middle: after it; right: one visit of four exposures minus the median of visits. The bright dot in the right panel is that same 7 MJy/sr cosmic-ray hit.

How to remove them

# visit = consecutive exposures of one detector, gap of less than half an hour
for pass, detector:                                 # at least three visits are needed
    img[v] = splat(visit v)                         # image of each visit on the sky grid
    ref    = percentile(img, 30, over visits)       # the sky as most visits see it
    for v:
        d    = gauss(img[v] - ref, 1 SPHEREx pixel);  d -= median(d)
        r    = gauss(ref, 1 SPHEREx pixel) - median
        core = grow(r > 5 * noise(r), 1 pixel)       # source cores are not checked
        odd  = ~core & (abs(d) > 2 * max(r, 0))      # a star's wing changes, but not by a factor of three
        area = connected(odd & (abs(d) > 3 * noise(d)))
        drop = [a for a in area if max(abs(d[a])) > 5 * noise(d)
                                and size(a) >= 16 SPHEREx pixels]
        for exp in visit v: exp.mask[drop] = False
  • The visit's pixels in the region found do not go into the stack. Other visits remain in their place; nothing is painted in.
  • The reference is the 30th percentile over visits, not the median. The streak is in almost half of the visits, and the median already carries part of it. The constant offset of the percentile relative to the sky is removed by subtracting the median of the difference.
  • Three conditions protect what is real. Source cores are not checked. In a star's wings the difference must be twice as large as the wing itself: a star legitimately changes from visit to visit along with the wavelength. Regions smaller than 16 pixels are left alone, so an asteroid visible in one visit stays.
  • Without the second condition the check eats out a ring in the halo of Barnard's Star: 22 thousand pixels. With it 321 are rejected there.
  • Result: ε Indi B field — 41 visits, 75 exposures, 5691 pixels (0.32%), 80% of them in D5 and D6; Barnard's Star field — 2 visits, 321 pixels (0.02%). The measured shifts of the targets did not change: 4.58 and 10.40″/yr.
  • Residual: the far end of the streak in D6 is still faintly visible in the video. In wide stacks (10′–60′ fields) this check is not applied: in a white frame the streak is fainter than the noise.
  • Code: visitclean.py, called from stack.py.

sections.title: What is marked on the picture
sections.html:
An object is given

Only it is marked: a marker on the object and the line of its path across the passes, one point per pass. Nothing else in the image is outlined. All the Barnard's Star videos are made this way.

Coordinates are given

Nothing is known about the field. The tool searches for everything that moves and marks only the tracks it found. This is the search between passes: on a 20′ field it found one track, and it is Barnard's Star. This search sees what moves from pass to pass. It does not see objects that cross the field in days; the blind search for such objects is described in the check on asteroids: on a field near the ecliptic it linked four tracks, and all four are known asteroids.

Check of the marker in the lab: for the five test targets at every field size the ring is within 0.3 pixel of the center of the saturated core (Barnard's Star, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or of the brightest source (ε Indi B), and the median offset between Gaia stars (G 9 to 14.5, moved to the SPHEREx epoch) and the peaks of the stacked image is at most 0.13 pixel (up to 283 stars).

sections.title: Test fields
sections.html:
Every step is shown on two targets, so that no algorithm is tuned to one object. The first is Barnard's Star: bright, saturated in every exposure, in a dense field of the Milky Way, moving 10.4″ per year. The second is ε Indi B, a pair of brown dwarfs 3.6 parsecs from us, moving across the sky by 4.7″ per year. It is the opposite of Barnard's Star: the object is faint, cold, does not saturate the detector and sits in an empty field far from the Milky Way. Every view is repeated on it with the same code; the second example is at the end of every section. A third field, one square degree on the ecliptic with 26 known asteroids, tests the search for objects that cross a field in days (field near the ecliptic).

  • The archive holds 445 exposures and four passes: April–June 2025, September–November 2025, April–May 2026, September–October 2026. The pipeline code is written for three passes, so the third one (74 exposures) is left out of the super-frames. The spectrum uses all four.
  • The coverage is uneven: detectors D1 and D4 have no exposures at all in the last pass. Only the detectors present in all three passes go into the white frame and the color: D2, D3, D5 and D6. Otherwise the brightness and color of the stars would change from pass to pass.
  • Narrow cutouts were not downloaded for this target: they are cropped locally from the 1° cutouts (crop.py). On Barnard's Star such a cutout matched the archive cutout pixel for pixel, including the coordinates and wavelengths.
  • The field has only five stars suitable for aligning the passes. The residual after alignment is 0.04–0.10″.
  • Saturation is computed only from the detectors of the white frame: D1 and D4 have three or four exposures per pass here, and a single flagged pixel would otherwise turn a spot far from any star white.
  • This target supplied the two hard cases of the cleaning: a faint streak in some of the D5 and D6 visits and a cosmic-ray hit shielded by a stronger one. Without steps 5 and 7 they show as red blotches around the object and a red dot next to it in the spectral-color picture.
  • What the second target required of the code: a saturated zone is one source in the blind search; exposures with no wavelength at the target position are skipped; the calibration on the wings is switched off for an unsaturated target.

sections.title: Pendulum
sections.html:
Three super-frames go back and forth. The background stays put, the target swings.

What you see and why

This is a blink comparator done honestly. Vision catches apparent motion when two frames differ only in the position of the object. So the whole job is to remove the other differences: the wavelength mix, the background, the brightness stretch, the pixel grid.

The order is 1→2→3→2 instead of 1→2→3→1: no return jump, which the eye reads as a separate motion.

The main view. The other views build on it.

How it is computed

  1. Take white[e] — the white super-frames of the passes (Super-frames, step 3). One stretch for all passes.
  2. Frame loop: hold 430 ms, crossfade 100 ms with t²(3−2t) easing. The rate is 2–3 Hz — the jump is most noticeable in this range.
  3. Only the target is marked: the marker sits on it, and a thin line with three points is its path across the passes. The line does not move and gives the eye an anchor.
  4. Next to it is a ×2.8 zoom inset, synchronized with the main field.
// fragment shader: three pass textures, a and b are the current pair
uniform sampler2D E[3]; uniform int a, b; uniform float mixT;
float s(float x){ return asinh((x-lo)/soft) / asinh((hi-lo)/soft); }
void main(){ float v = mix(s(texture(E[a],uv).r), s(texture(E[b],uv).r), mixT);
             color = vec4(vec3(v), 1.0); }

Pitfall: if a detector is missing in some pass, the white frame takes on a different “color” and the whole field starts to blink. Average only over the detectors that are present in all passes.

Second example: ε Indi B

Three super-frames: May 2025, October 2025, September 2026. The shift between the first and the last is 6.47″ over 1.41 years; the Gaia prediction with parallax is the same 6.47″. The middle pass is not halfway: five months passed from the first to the second, and a year from the second to the third.

sections.title: Spectral color
sections.html:
102 channels become the color of the object, not a slider.

What you see and why

This is how NASA draws the grid of brown dwarfs in its article about them: each layer of the cube is colored by its wavelength and everything is stacked. Hot stars come out blue-white, cold dwarfs orange and red, because they emit mostly at 4–5 µm.

For a motion search, color works like a passport. After the jump the eye matches the object to itself by color and does not confuse it with a neighbor. The cold object, which is what all of this is for, stands out even before it has moved.

It takes the place of a wavelength slider and is shown on top of the pendulum.

Cosmic-ray hits must be rejected before coloring. A hit is one pixel in one D6 exposure, tens of times brighter than its neighbors and absent in the frames two minutes before and after; in a color stack it shows as an isolated red dot that differs from pass to pass. The rejection of step 5 removes them.

How it is computed

def lam_rgb(lam):                      # rainbow: 0.75 µm violet → 5 µm red
    f_log = (ln(lam) - ln(0.74)) / (ln(5.02) - ln(0.74))
    f_lin = (lam - 0.74) / (5.02 - 0.74)
    h = 0.74 - 0.78 * (0.35*f_log + 0.65*f_lin)
    return hsv_to_rgb(h % 1, 0.88, 1.0)
for c in (R, G, B):                    # three stacks per pass
    chan[c] = splat(exposures, weight = lam_rgb(exp.lam)[c])
# white balance: a typical field star must be gray
kR = median(chan[G][stars] / chan[R][stars]);  kB = median(chan[G][stars] / chan[B][stars])
rgb = saturate(stretch(chan * [kR, 1, kB]), k = 2.4)
  • A cheap variant without re-stacking: a 3×6 matrix over the six detector stacks. It can be computed right in the shader.
  • stars — pixels brighter than 2.5 MJy/sr and no closer than 50″ to the target.

Pitfall: the image of a star is wider at long wavelengths, so a reddish ring appears around bright stars. The cure is PSF matching: the short-wavelength channels are convolved to the width of the long-wavelength ones.

Second example: ε Indi B

Here color works as intended. ε Indi B is orange-red, the field stars are white and bluish: most of the light of a cold dwarf comes near 4 µm. The white balance is set from the field stars, and there is no saturation. Why the color is what it is can be seen in the spectrum in the portrait.

sections.title: Wall of six detectors
sections.html:
The hint of the challenge statement taken literally: each detector is stacked separately, all six blink in sync.

What you see and why

A real object jumps in all six windows at the same time and by the same distance. A cosmic ray, a glint, a hot pixel or residual charge lives in one detector. Six witnesses who agree are more convincing than one bright one.

What these particular data show. Barnard's Star is visible in all six windows and has shifted by the same amount in each: 9.7–10.4″ (mean 10.1 ± 0.3″); Gaia gives 10.2″ for the same interval. The numbers on the right of the video are a measurement: in each exposure the center of the star is found by fitting a profile to the unsaturated pixels of the wings, and the median is taken per detector and pass (17–25 exposures). The error is 0.1–0.4″.

Only the target is marked on the panels: a marker on the star and the line of its path across the three passes. Outliers of single detectors are not circled: a mark on anything but the target draws the eye away from it.

The white disk at the center of each panel is saturation; there are no measurements there.

In the lab this is one of three views of a field, next to the single picture and the “Wall of bands” (one panel for each of the seven named bands: what the object is made of and in which light it is bright). Each panel of the wall of detectors carries the name of its range in words (very near infrared, near infrared, mid infrared), D1–D6 and the range in microns, with the number of exposures behind it. For a named target the shift between the first and the last pass is measured in every detector on the exposures of that detector (12 per detector and pass, taken evenly), and the line below the panels says how many of the six agree with the catalogue (or with each other, when the object has no catalogue motion). What the lab shows today: Barnard's Star 6 of 6, ε Indi B 6 of 6 (D4 has fewer exposures and a shorter baseline), RW Aurigae 6 of 6 (it does not move), WISE 0855−0714 1 of 6, R Draconis 3 of 6 (a saturated Mira, measured from its wings, with detectors missing in some passes).

How it is computed

  • Ranges: D1 0.75–1.10; D2 1.10–1.63; D3 1.63–2.42; D4 2.42–3.82; D5 3.82–4.42; D6 4.42–5.00 µm. The stack dets[e][k] of pass e and detector k is a product of the super-frames step.
  • Each panel has its own stretch, tied to the detector noise σ (median absolute deviation): lo = 0.5σ, hi = 4000σ, soft = 10σ.
  • One shared blink timer for all panels. Each panel has the target marker and the line of its path.
  • Automatic “consensus”: a candidate counts if its displacement agrees within the error in at least four panels out of six. For a named object with a proper motion the reference is the shift the catalogue gives for the same interval of each detector, with a floor of 1″ (all six detectors of Barnard's Star lie 0.6–0.9″ from the catalogue vector in right ascension, a common offset of registration and catalogue epoch, not a disagreement between detectors); for an object without one the reference is the median of the six detectors. A median alone would let a wrong majority win: WISE 0855−0714 is faint below 3.8 µm, the fits in D1–D4 settle on blended neighbours and agree on 4″ where the catalogue gives 8″; the catalogue accepts only D5 (7.4 ± 1.2″). The wall says so: “1 of 6 agree with the catalogue”.

The same wall can be retuned to molecules, as in the four-panel image of comet 3I/ATLAS: a panel is the sum of the frames with λ in the band minus the continuum from the neighboring channels.

BANDS = { 'H2O': (2.50, 3.05), 'CH4': (3.10, 3.60), 'CO2': (4.20, 4.35), 'CO': (4.45, 4.90) }
line_map = splat(exps in band) - 0.5 * (splat(exps just below) + splat(exps just above))

Second example: ε Indi B

Shift by detector: D2 6.30 ± 0.12″, D3 6.36 ± 0.10″, D5 6.56 ± 0.09″, D6 6.52 ± 0.07″; from Gaia 6.47″. The D1 and D4 windows are empty in the last pass: SPHEREx has not yet looked there with these detectors. This is what uneven coverage looks like in fresh data, and the wall shows it at once.

sections.title: Nested fields of view
sections.html:
Speed rings suggest which field you need.

What you see and why

The challenge item about choosing the field of view. The user does not know in advance which field they need, because they do not know the speed of the object. The rings answer this directly: the “30″/yr” ring shows how far an object with that speed will go in the time between the first and the last pass.

A small field shows what is slow, a large one catches what is fast. The counter on the right counts only the useful layers (image, flags, variance): with a large field they really are hundreds of times larger.

But the real download hardly depends on the field. An IRSA cutout drags the PSF along (about 5 MB) at any size. Measured on our downloads: a 7′ cutout weighs 4.7 MB, 20′ — 5.4 MB, 1° — 9.6 MB; 359 cutouts of 1° took 3.4 GB. A small field pays off only when the server reads the pixels itself and leaves the PSF behind; the sky service of this project does that (it reads only the image rows it needs from the public copy of the archive). All frames of this video are stacks of all 359 exposures downloaded with a 1° field.

For scale: an object at 500 au swings by ±7′ over half a year because of parallax. Planet X needs a field of at least 15′.

How it is computed

dt = t_last - t_first                    # years
for v in (1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300):       # ″/yr
    r_px = v * dt * panel_px / fov_arcsec
    if 14 < r_px < panel_px * 0.72: draw_ring(centre, r_px, label = v)
n_pix  = fov_arcsec / 6.15               # side of the cutout in pixels
bytes  = n_exp * n_pix**2 * 12           # useful layers: image + flags + variance, 4 bytes each
# with an IRSA cutout the actual download is ≈ n_exp * 5 MB at any fov (PSF inside)
v_max  = fov_arcsec / 2 / dt             # faster than this, the object leaves the frame
  • Wide fields are stacked the same way as narrow ones, by pass and detector with the same kernel. The grid step is chosen so that the picture is about a thousand grid pixels across: 1.54″ (a quarter of a SPHEREx pixel) up to the 20′ field (800 × 800), 3.07″ (half a pixel) for the 60′ field (1200 × 1200). A finer grid on 60′ would hold more than a screen shows; the detail comes back when the field is narrowed.
  • In the video the transition between the wide and the narrow stack is a smooth blend in the range 5′–3.8′.
  • The field is part of the address of the lab (#/lab?ra=…&dec=…&fov=…), so any view opens by a link: the challenge item about coordinates in the URL.

Second example: ε Indi B

ε Indi B, at 4.6″/yr, lies between the 3 and 10″/yr rings. In the 20′ field, ε Indi A also enters the frame.
