sections.title: Difference between passes and the artifact mask
sections.html:
Two more ways to look at the same stacks. Both are in the lab.

Difference

A per-pixel significance map of every pass against the first one. For each band, z = (D − S) / √(σ² + σ₁² + (0.05·max(|a|, |b|))²), where a and b are the values of the pixel in the first pass and in the pass shown (after the sky subtraction of each exposure), D = b − a, σ₁ and σ are the noise of the stacked pixel in the two passes (1/√Σw), and S is the smooth part of D: the median of the valid pixels in 24-pixel windows on an 8-pixel grid, interpolated bilinearly. The last term under the root is an assumed 5 % floor for the differences of PSF, calibration and wavelength sampling between passes; without it a bright star would dominate the map.

S removes the change of the diffuse sky level between passes: zodiacal light changes with the viewing geometry and is not a change of any source. It also removes real extended change larger than about 2.5′.

Several bands are combined as a Stouffer sum Σz/√m, where m counts the bands that have exposures in both passes (the dust window lies inside the methane window and shares its exposures, so the two count as one). Pixels with |z| above 4 are colored, cyan where the source is fainter and magenta where it is brighter, saturating at |z| = 10. For independent Gaussian noise about one pixel in 16,000 exceeds this threshold by chance; real noise is not Gaussian, so an isolated colored pixel is not a detection. The first pass is the reference and shows nothing.

Calibration of the noise. The noise model above is a model, and on real stacks it was wrong: the stacks are smoothed (neighbouring pixels are not independent), a pass with few exposures per detector is noisier than 1/√Σw says, and the weights change across the field (ε Indi B, pass 3 of 4: 11.9 % of the field above |z| = 4, width of z on empty sky 2.2 for the white frame and up to 4.4 for single bands, where Gaussian noise gives 0.006 %). Now the noise term σ is multiplied by the robust width (1.4826 × MAD) of (D − S)/σ, measured in the same 24-pixel windows as S on the pixels that have no source in either pass (a source is a pixel more than 2 robust widths above the 15 × 15 median of its frame, dilated by 2 detector pixels). The 5 % floor is not scaled: it is a statement about flux, not about noise. On empty sky the width of z is then 1 by construction (measured on the white frame: 0.93–1.05 in every pass of ε Indi B and Barnard’s Star), and a source that changed stands out of it. What this does not do: z has heavy tails where static stars differ between passes (different roll angle, wavelength sampling, PSF): 93–98 % of the area above |z| = 4 lies in blobs of 12 pixels or more, the isolated rest is 0.02–0.06 % of the field (0.15–0.22 % in two passes of Barnard’s Star). The Stouffer sum over a chosen subset of bands assumes independent bands; they share exposures, so its width on empty sky is 1.1–1.25, not 1. With all bands chosen the view uses the white frame, which is the calibrated one.

Limit. Passes sample different wavelengths, so every star differs somewhat between them: a colored star is not by itself a variable, and a change is claimed only at matched wavelengths (section “Object card”). Sharp edges of bright diffuse structure show for the same reason.

Artifact mask

Per pixel, the fraction of the exposures in which it carries a bad flag (groups 1, 4 and 8 of the table in “Pixel values, units and flags”), drawn in red over the Starlight image. Pixels outside the footprint of an exposure are not counted, so the mask shows artifacts, not coverage. It answers one question about any feature of a picture: did the SPHEREx pipeline flag this place, and in how many exposures.

In the lab the mask is a checkbox of the Display options. The flag word of every exposure is read in full (the names come from the flag table of the file itself); for each pixel the service keeps, for every flag name that is set in at least 2 % of the exposures somewhere in the field, the share of the exposures that carry it. The red of the mask combines the shares of the flags that mark a bad pixel (phantom, reference, non-functional, missing data, hot, cold, outlier, snowball, transient, overflow, SUR_ERROR, persistence) as 1 − Π(1 − share), as if they were independent. With the pointer over the picture the flags of the pixel that are set in at least 5 % of the exposures are listed with their shares (for example “SOURCE 100 % · SUR_ERROR 71 % · BLOOM 65 %”); SOURCE and BLOOM are listed but do not redden the mask.

sections.title: Time machine: archive images
sections.html:
Images from other telescopes in the same projection: 76 years of one star.

What you see and why

A year of SPHEREx observations gives a shift of one and a half pixels. Archives give decades: since 1950 Barnard's Star has moved 13 arcminutes. A candidate found in SPHEREx is checked in a second: we extend its motion backward and see whether it is at the right place in the old images.

Two views at once. On the left the sky is fixed and the star creeps upward. On the right the camera travels with the star: the star is in the center and the background drifts away. The second view is good when the shift between images is larger than the field of view.

Used: POSS-I 1950, Quick-V 1982, POSS-II 1988/1991/1993, 2MASS 2000, WISE 2010, Pan-STARRS 2012, SPHEREx 2025–2026.

Check: the date of each image is confirmed by the FITS headers (for 2MASS and WISE there are no dates in the files; they are taken from the survey descriptions). The star sits at the point predicted from Gaia to within 0.3″ in 2MASS, 0.6″ in Quick-V, 1.7″ in WISE and 2.8–3.7″ on the POSS plates. In the Pan-STARRS image the star is saturated and artifacts remain around it, so the center cannot be measured there: this is labeled in the video.

How it is computed

# DSS (plate scans), date in the DATE-OBS header
https://archive.stsci.edu/cgi-bin/dss_search?v=poss1_red&r={ra}&d={dec}&e=J2000&h={arcmin}&w={arcmin}&f=fits
#   v = poss1_red | poss1_blue | quickv | poss2ukstu_blue | poss2ukstu_red | poss2ukstu_ir
# 2MASS, WISE, SDSS, DSS in one query: XML with links to the FITS files and dates
https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/applications/finderchart/servlet/api?mode=prog&locstr={ra}+{dec}&subsetsize={arcmin}&survey=2mass,wise,dss,sdss
# Pan-STARRS
https://ps1images.stsci.edu/cgi-bin/ps1filenames.py?ra={ra}&dec={dec}&filters=izy
https://ps1images.stsci.edu/cgi-bin/fitscut.cgi?ra={ra}&dec={dec}&size={px}&format=fits&red={filename}
# reprojection onto our grid
x, y = WCS(header).celestial.all_world2pix(grid_ra, grid_dec, 0)
img  = map_coordinates(data, [y, x], order = 1)
# images of different nature: percentile stretch
lo, hi = percentile(img, 40), percentile(img, 99.85)
s = asinh((img - lo)/(hi - lo)/0.06) / asinh(1/0.06)
  • Position for the “tracking camera”: a straight line through the measured SPHEREx passes, extended backward, or the proper motion from Gaia.
  • The images are taken directly from STScI and IRSA. The services of CDS (the hips2fits cutouts, the tiles behind Aladin Lite) would give the same surveys with less code; they did not respond from our network.

Second example: ε Indi B

A cold dwarf in the archives over 48 years. On the blue plate of 1978 the predicted position is empty (1.5σ). On the red plate of 1993 the answer is ambiguous: a diffraction spike from ε Indi A passes nearby. On the infrared plate of 1997 the object is there: 26σ, 0.9″ from the prediction. In 2MASS (2000) and WISE (2010) it is bright, 0.3″ and 0.5″ from the prediction. The 2MASS image is cut off by the edge of its tile, so half of the frame is black.

sections.title: Object portrait
sections.html:
A cube of 102 layers, a color thumbnail and a spectrum on the fly, after the NASA illustration for the article about brown dwarfs.

What you see and why

In the NASA article the object is shown as three things side by side: a pile of layers by wavelength, a color thumbnail and a rainbow spectrum with molecular bands. Here this is made live. The layers flip through by themselves, and each exposure, as it goes by, puts its own point on the spectrum. Then the layers are stacked into a “passport” color, and the thumbnail starts to blink through the passes.

The object stays in place while the layers flip: the frames of all three passes are shifted so that the target is in the center. Otherwise the star would be smeared over its own proper motion.

The spectrum here is a rough draft and mostly shows the overall slope. Scatter of the points around the running median: 20–25% in D2–D3 and 5–6% in D4–D6. At the D4/D5 and D5/D6 joins there are steps of ×0.6 and ×0.7, which a real spectrum cannot have: these are traces of the calibration on a saturated star. The water dips at 1.4 and 1.9 µm are hinted at (about 25% below the neighboring regions, roughly 1.5σ); at 2.7 µm they are not visible.

This spectrum cannot be recomputed the way the check below measures an unsaturated star: around a star this bright the files contain no pixels that can be trusted at the percent level. The three attempts and their numbers are in the section “where to be careful”. The curve in the video is the estimate from the wings, a rough draft.

The blackbody estimate of about 3500 K against the catalog 3200 K was obtained from this same curve and is not good to better than ±300 K. The value of the video is the card interface, not the spectrum measurement. For unsaturated objects the calibration on the bright wings is not needed, and the accuracy is different: the check on an ordinary star below gives a scatter of 1–4% and detector joins without steps.

Object card: opens on a click on any source.

How it is computed

# 1. cube in the object's frame: each frame is shifted by the target position in its own pass
u, v = sky_to_grid(...) + (c_mean - c[epoch(exp)])
# 2. layer at wavelength lam0: sliding window in ln λ, 56 steps from 0.76 to 4.95 µm
w = exp(-(ln(exp.lam) - ln(lam0))**2 / (2 * 0.05**2));  use frames with w > 0.03
slice[lam0] = splat(exposures, weight = w, sigma = 0.42 native px, comoving = True)
show = stretch(slice) * (0.25 + 0.75 * lam_rgb(lam0))
# 3. a spectrum point from each exposure
#    ordinary object: PSF fit in a 7×7 window, see the check below
#    saturated object: wings only               (1 MJy/sr × 6.15″ pixel = 0.889 mJy)
ann  = sum(median(img[ring]) * area(ring) for ring in rings(2.8..6.0 px, step 0.4))
flux = K(lam) * ann * 0.889e-3     # K is a parabola in ln λ: ratio of the PSF amplitude to the flux in the annulus
# 4. temperature: blackbody curve in log flux
T = argmin_T sum( (ln F_i - ln(a_T * B_nu(lam_i, T)))**2 ),  T = 2000..5000 K, step 25
  • Bands for highlighting (yellow in the video): H₂O 1.33–1.50, 1.75–2.05, 2.50–3.05; CH₄ 3.1–3.6; CO₂ 4.2–4.35; CO 2.29–2.42 and 4.35–4.95 µm.
  • The spectra of the three passes are drawn together. If they coincide, the object is not variable. If not, that is a separate finding.
  • The spectrum is computed on the server together with the stacks and returned in the same response: 358 numbers.

Second example: ε Indi B

The core is not saturated, so each point is an ordinary PSF fit in a single exposure, without calibration on the wings. The spectrum has three peaks near 1.3, 1.6 and 2.1 µm, deep dips between them and a large peak at 4 µm. This is what a cold dwarf with water and methane in its atmosphere looks like; field stars have a smooth decline at this place. Diamonds are catalogs: the flux is 0.93 of 2MASS in J and H and 0.99 in Ks.

sections.title: Spectrum on click: the check on an ordinary star
sections.html:
The same technique as in the portrait, but on a star without saturation and with a cross-check against the 2MASS and WISE catalogs.

Why

Motion says that the object is nearby. The spectrum says what the object is. Without it a candidate remains a dot that moved. Three cases have to be told apart: a star (a peak near 1.6 µm and a smooth decline, as here), a cold dwarf or a planet (methane and water bands, a rise toward 4–5 µm), an asteroid (reflected sunlight and a thermal rise beyond 3.5 µm).

The second benefit is a check of the source itself. For a real object the points of three passes fall on one curve.

The test and its result

The star 2MASS J17572542+0446559 (Gaia DR3 4472836601996372992), J = 11.53, 5.6′ from Barnard's Star. It was chosen on three conditions: the core is not saturated, neighbors within 28″ give about 1% of its flux, and it fell in 358 exposures out of 359. According to Gaia it is a distant red giant (BP−RP = 1.47, parallax 0.15 mas).

The video runs in the order of observation. On the left are the stack of the field and the pixels of the current exposure around the star, with no rotation and no smoothing. Below the plot is the fit itself: pixels, model, residual. Each exposure puts one point on the plot.

The 358 exposures gave 347 points. Two were skipped because of the overflow flag in the core, eight because of bad pixels in the core, and one point fell out of line with its neighbors. Scatter around the running median: 1.1–2.6% in D1–D4 and 3.4–3.9% in D5–D6. At the five detector boundaries the curve agrees to within 0.95–1.02.

BandCatalogSpectrumRatio
2MASS J, 1.24 µm38.9 mJy38.2 mJy0.98
2MASS H, 1.66 µm45.6 mJy45.1 mJy0.99
2MASS Ks, 2.16 µm32.7 mJy33.4 mJy1.02
WISE W1, 3.35 µm16.5 mJy16.1 mJy0.98
WISE W2, 4.60 µm8.4 mJynot compared: the band extends to 5.3 µm, SPHEREx ends at 5.0

The same on ten isolated stars with J from 10.8 to 12.9: 40 comparisons, median ratio 0.98, scatter 3%, worst discrepancy 7%. The points of the third pass, where the PSF is stored in a different format, differ from the first two by 0.5–5%.

On five faint stars with J from 14.1 to 15.2 the noise of one point is 0.05–0.15 mJy. 14 comparisons out of 20 agree with the catalog to within 10%, the worst discrepancy is 18%: in a field this crowded the neighbors interfere.

Spectrum on click works on an ordinary source: the fluxes agree with the catalogs to within a few percent.

How it is done

# one exposure → one spectrum point
ra_t, dec_t = object position at the frame date       # click + proper motion or track
x, y      = WCS(hdr).all_world2pix(ra_t, dec_t, 0)
lam, dlam = WCS(hdr, fobj=hdul, key='W').all_pix2world(x, y, 0)
stamp = IMAGE[y-3:y+4, x-3:x+4];  var = VARIANCE[same window]    # 7×7 pixels
ok    = finite(stamp) & !(flags & BAD)
if the core (r < 1.6 px) has OVERFLOW or NaN:  skip the exposure
psf = PSF of the detector zone, shifted by the fractional part of (x, y), at pixel centers
      # PSF cube (QR2, ×10): first convolve with the 10×10 pixel square
      # EPSF table (QR3, ×5): already integrated over the pixel
A, B = argmin sum( ok * (stamp - A*psf - B)**2 / var )            # linear 2×2 problem
up to 3 times: ok &= |stamp - A*psf - B| < 6*sqrt(var + (0.1*A*psf)**2);  solve again
flux_Jy = A * omega_pix * 1e6                                     # omega_pix ≈ 8.89e-10 sr
# spectrum: the points of all exposures by lam
# a point farther than 5σ from the median of its seven neighbors in lam is dropped
  • No catalog is needed; the input is the click coordinates. For a moving object the position is taken at the date of each frame: from the proper motion (here from Gaia) or from the track. On real moving objects this is tested in the next section.
  • The PSF pitfall. The PSF cube from QR2 is the optical profile on a fine grid. Taken as is, it gives fluxes on average 8% below the catalogs. It has to be integrated over the pixel area. The EPSF table from QR3 is already integrated.
  • The bright limit. A pixel gets the overflow flag from about 70–90 MJy/sr in D1–D3 and from 50 in D4. A star with J = 9.4 loses 194 exposures out of 348 to this, a star with J = 10.8 loses 12 out of 345. Sources fainter than J ≈ 10.5 are measured reliably this way. If pixels with this flag are allowed, stars as bright as J ≈ 8.5 still agree with 2MASS to within 0–6%; for brighter ones the flux is underestimated by 4–13%.
  • The background is a constant in the same 7×7 window. A neighbor inside the window spoils the point; the only protection against this is the rejection of pixels by their residual.
  • Speed: 358 exposures are processed in 10 seconds on one core from files on disk. In the web application the time goes into reading the exposures, so the spectrum is computed from the same exposures that are already read for the picture.
  • Cross-check: the spectrum is averaged under the filter transmission curve and compared with the flux F0 · 10^(−0.4·m); the zero points are 1594, 1024, 666.7 Jy for J, H, Ks and 309.5 Jy for W1.
  • Code: spec.py (the measurement, about a hundred lines), speccheck.py (the cross-check), vids_g.py (this video). A ready-made replacement for the hand-written fit is photutils.psf.

Second example: ε Indi B

The same spectrum over all four passes: 444 exposures, 414 points. Cross-check against the catalogs: 0.91 in J, 0.93 in H, 0.99 in Ks and 1.20 in W1. The discrepancy is larger than for ordinary stars (2–3%). Possible reasons: the catalog measurements were made in 1999 and 2010; the spectrum is very steep inside the bands; W1 is flagged in the catalog as contaminated by the halo of ε Indi A. Which of them is the main one has not been checked.

In the lab today: the same fit, on the service

The lab no longer sums an aperture. A click (or the named target) asks the service for the spectrum: for every exposure that holds the place it reads a small window around it (about 100 arcseconds, from the same files and the same window cache as the pictures, with the VARIANCE plane), fits flux · PSF + sky on the 7 × 7 stamp with the PSF of the detector zone, and returns one point per exposure. The Spectrum tab, the Object card and its change test use these points; the field can be of any size because the window does not come from the field.

Clicking a place, or the named target, gives one point per exposure at that place's wavelength, measured by the service (/api/field_spectrum, engine/photometry.py, the port of spec.py): a 7 × 7 stamp around the position of the object in that exposure; the model flux · PSF + sky (the PSF of the detector zone, shifted to the sub-pixel position, pixel-integrated: the QR2 cube is integrated over the pixel, the QR3 table already is), fitted by weighted least squares with the weights 1 / VARIANCE; three rounds of 6σ rejection of pixels (the allowance includes 10 % of the model for the mismatch of the PSF); the point is skipped when a pixel of the core (within 1.6 pixels) has the overflow flag or no value, or when the stamp has fewer than 20 usable pixels; a point whose PSF stands on less than 80 % good pixels is dropped; and a point that is more than 5 robust sigma from the median of its seven neighbours in wavelength is dropped. Flux = amplitude × the solid angle of the pixel (from the local WCS) in Jy; the error is the formal error of the fit. For the named target of the field and for a moving body the stamp is put where the object is in that exposure (proper motion and parallax for a star; the positions of a track, interpolated in time, for a body). A clicked position that is not a catalogued source is a fixed position on the sky. Nothing is corrected for the aperture: the PSF fit measures the total flux.

The second chart is not a light curve: it is the flux ratio of the later to the earlier season at matched wavelengths (the bins of “Does it change?”, see Object card), with error bars that include the assumed 3 % floor and a line at 1. A seasonal mean of one window is not shown, because seasons sample different wavelengths there and a red source then appears to brighten or fade by tens of per cent without any change. When a point is on a seam between cubes (mosaic) no chart is drawn.

Limit. A point has the sampling of the real archive: a handful of exposures per season at scattered wavelengths, not 102 channels per season. A saturated source (Barnard's Star, R Draconis) gives no calibrated spectrum: when the core is saturated in more than half of the exposures the card and the Spectrum tab say so instead of drawing a curve.

sections.title: Object card
sections.html:
The Object panel describes the target (or any source you click). Position, distance, motion and brightness come from catalogs, not from SPHEREx; SPHEREx supplies the exposure counts and the brightness by season.

  • Selection: a click picks the nearest source of the field's own list (the sources the data show, S/N 7 or more or saturated, within 14 screen pixels of the click) whether or not a catalogue knows it; the catalogue match (SIMBAD, Gaia within 4″ at the date of the source) only names it. A click on empty sky says so and offers a spectrum at that place. The named target is looked for at its predicted place and the card says “Not detected” when no source stands there (WISE 0855).
  • Distance: 1000 / parallax (pc) × 3.26156 light-years, using the Gaia DR3 parallax only when RUWE ≤ 1.4 and parallax ≥ 3 mas (Gaia's error is about 0.1 mas for G < 17.5, so this is a 20σ or better measurement; the zero-point correction of a few hundredths of a mas is not applied); otherwise a SIMBAD parallax is used for the target and labelled less certain, and a clicked star gets no distance. One exception, by name: for RW Aurigae SIMBAD's basic parallax (15.42 mas, 212 light-years) is too large; the lab and the Findings page use the Gaia DR3 parallax of RW Aur A, 6.41 mas (RUWE 1.5, a close pair, so indicative; about 510 light-years). The Gaia source that the lab matches at that position is RW Aur B (G 13.04, RUWE 16.4), and the card says so; there is no general rule for this yet. “Light in these exposures left in” is the year of the last season minus the distance in light-years (shown only below 1,500 light-years).
  • Motion: proper motion √(μα*² + μδ²) from Gaia, or SIMBAD without a Gaia match; pixels per year = μ / 6.15″. Speed across the sky = 4.74047 · μ(″/yr) / parallax(″) km/s (tangential only).
  • Saturation: exposures with an overflow flag or a missing value in the core are not fitted (see the spectrum rule above); if more than half of the exposures are like that the star is called too bright and no calibrated spectrum is made.
  • Brightness by season: mean ± standard error of the clean 0.75–1.1 µm points per season (at least 5 per season; error = sample standard deviation with n − 1, divided by √n); a season is “detected” only if the mean exceeds 3 × its own error. These per-season means are no longer shown on the Object card, because they invite a false light curve; only the matched test is.
  • Does it change? (matched wavelengths): exposures of different seasons sample the spectrum at different wavelengths, so only exposures in the same resolution element are compared: the wavelength axis is cut at the detector boundaries (1.11, 1.64, 2.42, 3.82, 4.42 µm) and, inside each detector, into bins of width λ/R (R = 41 for D1–D3, 35 for D4, 110 for D5, 130 for D6; ln-spaced from the detector's lower edge) and every good point falls into one bin of its season, keyed by the exposure's own detector number (a point outside the nominal range of its detector goes into that detector's nearest bin). Per bin and season the inverse-variance mean flux and its error are formed. For the pair of seasons (earliest and latest that share at least 3 bins) zi = (Fb − Fa)/√(σa² + σb² + (0.03·√(Fa² + Fb²))²), where the last term is an assumed 3 % relative-calibration floor (not a measured value); χ² = Σzi² with dof = number of bins (no parameter is fitted). The error of the weighted mean ratio is multiplied by √(χ²/dof) when that exceeds 1 (excess scatter). A change is stated only if the Wilson–Hilferty normal equivalent of χ² exceeds 4, the error-weighted mean ratio Fb/Fa differs from 1 by more than 10 %, and the flux is above 3σ in both seasons at the shared bins; otherwise “no change found” (with the ratio and its error, the median and largest per-bin |z| and χ²/dof) or “not detected”. A χ²/dof well above 1 with a small ratio means that individual bins differ by more than the assumed floor; the cause can be wavelength-dependent calibration, the PSF, real variability of the source (brown dwarfs and giants vary), or the pipeline version (the exposures of one field mix versions v20, v24 and v27 without cross-calibration, and the 3 % floor is not a measured bound on that). Within a bin the spectrum is assumed flat, which is a poor assumption inside a strong absorption band of a cool dwarf. Because most targets are faint in single exposures, “no change found” means “no change larger than the stated error”.
  • Tiers: A a Gaia DR3 star with clean astrometry (RUWE ≤ 1.4), a parallax of at least 3 mas and no saturation; B identified but saturated, without a clean Gaia match, with RUWE > 1.4 or with a small parallax (distance not stated); C no catalogued source within 2.5 pixels (only brightness can be said, never a molecule, a temperature or a distance).
  • Published facts (planets, temperatures, periods) are copied from the cited papers for the test targets only and are labelled as published; they are not measured here.
  • Not derived: temperature, molecules, feature depths. A model fit with stated limits is planned.

sections.title: The search between passes in the lab
sections.html:
When the service has built a field with at least three passes it runs the search between passes on the white stack of every pass (engine/search.py, the port of detect.py; result at /api/field_search?key&kind=passes). Nothing about the object of the field is passed in: the same search runs on a field opened by name and on one opened by coordinates.

  • Sources of a pass. Local maxima of the stack smoothed to the size of a point source (7″ FWHM), above 8 robust sigma; inside the halo of a bright star a source must stand above the halo itself (8 sigma over the halo and 3 times the halo light), because diffraction spikes and rings turn with the roll angle of the telescope between passes and imitate motion. Only where every pass has a value, 20″ in from the edge of that area. A saturated zone is one source at its centre, however wide its flat top is (zones smaller than one detector pixel are not stars).
  • Standing still. A source is stationary when every other pass has a source within 2.5″ of it. The rest are moving candidates.
  • Tracks. The first and the last pass fix a velocity (3 to 120″ per year); the places in the passes between are predicted, and a source within 2.5″ of the prediction in at least one of them (brightness within a factor 2.5) makes a track of at least three passes; the velocity is then refitted on the members. Two tracks through the same sources are one.
  • Afterwards: Gaia. Every Gaia DR3 star with a proper motion above 2 mas/yr is moved to the date of each pass; if one is within 3″ of the track in every pass the card says so (“a star with a high proper motion”). A track that no Gaia star explains is “unexplained”, which is not “new”: it can be a faint red dwarf or a brown dwarf without a Gaia motion (ε Indi B is one), a distant body or an artifact.

On the lab's own test fields: RA 269.4479, Dec +4.7687, 5′ (coordinates only): one track, 10.5″/yr at position angle 353° in all three passes, and Gaia names it as Barnard's Star (G 8.19, 10.39″/yr). At 20′ the same field has 343 sources and again one track. RA 331.077, Dec −56.794, 5′: one track of 4.5″/yr through all four passes, unexplained by Gaia: the brown dwarf ε Indi B.

Limits. Fewer than three passes give no search (the card says so). A body that moves less than 3″ or more than 120″ per year between passes is not linked; a body that is in only two passes is not a track. A source on the diffraction spike of a very bright star can still be linked when the roll angle repeats.

sections.title: Portrait, check against catalogues and thermal signature (in the lab)
sections.html:
Three things come with the spectrum of a clicked object (service: /api/field_spectrum, /api/field_layers; code: engine/photometry.py, engine/portrait.py).

  • The portrait. 56 layers from 0.76 to 4.95 µm, equally spaced in ln λ. An exposure has one wavelength at the object, so layer L takes every exposure with the weight exp(−(ln λ − ln λL)² / (2 · 0.05²)); an exposure with a weight below 0.03 does not count. Every exposure is put on a small grid (64 × 64 pixels of 1.54″, 98″ wide) co-moving: the object, at its own position in that exposure, is at the centre, so a star is not smeared over its proper motion and a body does not streak. The sky of one exposure is the clipped median of its window; pixels with a bad flag, an overflow or no value are left out; the sums are smoothed once with σ = 0.42 native pixel. The thumbnail adds the layers with the rainbow colour of their wavelength, per pixel over the layers that have a value, so that a flat spectrum is white. The layers flip by themselves on the Spectrum tab, a line on the spectrum marks the layer on show, and a slider lets you stop on one. A layer with few exposures says so.
  • The check against catalogues. The cleaned spectrum is averaged under the filter curves of 2MASS J, H, Ks and WISE W1, W2 (photon counting; the curves are in motion_pipeline/cat/filters) and compared with the flux F0 · 10−0.4 m of the catalogue magnitude (zero points 1594, 1024, 666.7 Jy and 309.5, 171.8 Jy). The magnitudes come from IRSA (fp_psc, allwise_p3as_psd) at the position moved back to each survey's epoch; a band is used only when its quality letter is A or B, and a source with a neighbour of similar brightness within 8″ is a blend and gets no check. A band the spectrum does not cover without a hole is left out. On ε Indi B the ratios are 0.92 (J), 0.94 (H), 0.98 (Ks) and 1.18 (W1): the catalogues were made in 1999 and 2010 and the spectrum is steep inside the bands.
  • The thermal signature of a moving body. The ratio of the mean flux at 3.82–4.42 µm to the mean flux at 1.10–1.63 µm of the cleaned on − off spectrum (at least four points in each range); the card shows the ratio with its error and the ratio of sunlight reflected by a grey surface (a 5772 K blackbody: about 0.23) beside it. A ratio clearly above that says the body shines by its own heat. For a body that moves, on − off is: the PSF flux at the place where the body was at the time of each exposure, minus the median of the nine nearest in wavelength of the fluxes at the same sky place in exposures of the same detector taken at least two days before or after the track (at most 240 of them, spread evenly in time); with fewer than four such references a point has no value. A track longer than 10′ is measured without the off-exposures.

Limits. The thermal ratio mixes reflected light and heat, and a body's colour changes with its rotation, so it is a hint, not a temperature. The portrait is a sum of exposures of different dates (a variable object is blurred in time), and its thickness depends on how many exposures fall near each wavelength.

sections.title: The time machine: archive images of the same sky
sections.html:
The lab shows what the same place looked like before SPHEREx (service: /api/archive). The images come from: the Digitized Sky Surveys (STScI; the POSS-I, POSS-II and UK Schmidt plates, up to five variants, from 1950), 2MASS J, H, Ks (IRSA Finder Chart, 1997–2001), AllWISE W1, W2 (IRSA Finder Chart, 2010), Pan-STARRS g, i (STScI cutout service, a stack of 2010–2014; the cutout carries no date of the stack, so it is dated “2010–2014”). The date of a plate is read from its header (the time of the plates is written as hours and hundredths of an hour), that of 2MASS and WISE from the service's table.

Every image is reprojected to a grid of its own over the field (the field's centre, at most 600 pixels, the step of the super-frames up to 20′): the sphere is cut into the grid's pixels, the image is smoothed to the grid's pixel when it is finer, and sampled bilinearly; a place that the image does not reach is “no data”. Each image is stretched by itself (asinh between its 0.5 and 99.7 per cent) and tinted by the wavelength of its band. The result is cached. Sky fixed: the stars stay, a ring marks the object where it was on that date (its proper motion times the years since the field was centred). Camera on the object: the image is moved by the object's proper motion, so the object stays at the centre and the stars drift. Nothing is drawn as if it were a SPHEREx exposure: the survey, the band, the date and the credit are written on the image.

Limits. An image can be missing (the plates of POSS-I stop at declination −30°, Pan-STARRS at −30° too; 2MASS tiles end at an edge: the black strip is not an artifact of the lab); the service says which survey did not answer. A fast star can leave the field between two surveys.

sections.title: Everything that moves: the search between passes
sections.html:
Coordinate mode: no object is given, the tool looks for motion by itself.

What you see and why

The user entered coordinates, not a name. The search is given only three stacks of a 20′ field; it knows nothing about Barnard's Star. It finds the sources in each pass, discards the ones that stay in place, and tries to link the rest into straight-line tracks.

Result on these data: about 470 sources per pass, 460 stationary, one track. Its speed is 9.98″/yr, direction 352°. Only this track is marked.

This is why the cosmic-ray rejection of step 5 comes before the search: without it single-exposure hits blink in the stacks, and one of them (596 MJy/sr in a single D6 exposure) produces a false second track at 4.3″/yr. With the rejection nothing in the field changes except the target. The search did not match four sources of the first pass to the other passes: these are either sources right at the detection threshold or close pairs of stars; the sky brightness at these places is the same in all three passes.

The catalog cross-check comes only after the search: according to Gaia DR3, Barnard's Star is at this place, 10.41″/yr toward 356° over the same interval. The positions found differ from the Gaia prediction by 0.7″ in all three passes. The saturated zone of the star counts as one source centered in the middle of the zone; taking the peak on its flat top instead gives 10.22″/yr.

The limit of the method. On a 1° field the same search finds the same track (9.6″/yr), but with loose thresholds it adds up to four false ones: 3–6″/yr at faint sources and at a saturated bright star in the corner. With the thresholds “brighter than 15σ and faster than 5″/yr” one real track remains. What matters is not the speed but the shift between the first and the last pass: ε Indi B, moving at 4.5″/yr, was caught on a 1.4-year baseline, when the shift had grown to 6.5″. This search does not reliably catch a shift smaller than about 5″.

How it is computed

# input: three stacks E[e] on one grid, times t[e] in years; saturation = 1500 MJy/sr
def sources(img):                         # sources of one pass
    sm = gauss(img, 0.7 * sigma_psf)      # FWHM PSF 7″
    peaks = local_maxima(sm, box = 3 * FWHM) where sm - halo > 8 * MAD and sm - halo > 3 * hl
    out = [centroid(img, p) for p in peaks if covered_by_all_stacks(p) and not saturated(p)]
    out += [centre(z) for z in real_saturated_zones]      # a saturated zone is one source
    return out
S = [sources(E[e]) for e in passes]
moving[e] = [p for p in S[e] if not (neighbor closer than 2.5″ in both other passes)]
tracks = []
for p0 in moving[0]:
    for p2 in moving[2]:
        v = (p2 - p0) / t[2]                          # ″/yr
        if not 3 <= |v| <= 120: continue
        expect = p0 + v * t[1]                        # where the object should be in the middle pass
        for p1 in moving[1]:
            if |p1 - expect| < 2.5″ and brightnesses agree within a factor of 2.5:
                tracks.append((p0, p1, p2, v))
  • Sources are searched for only where the sky is covered by all detectors in all passes. Otherwise the different set of frames near the field edge looks like motion.
  • A saturated star is one source at the center of its zone. Peaks on its flat top come in dozens and link into false tracks: ε Indi A had more than two thousand of them. Near a bright star the contrast rule from step 6 applies.
  • The 2.5″ tolerance on the middle pass leaves room for parallax: for Barnard's Star the deviation from a straight line is 1.0″.
  • Only the elements of tracks are drawn on the image: a marker on the object and a line through its three positions. Stationary sources and candidates without a track are not marked; their number is shown by a counter.
  • For each track, a query to Gaia by position and velocity. A match gives a name; no match is a reason to look closely.
  • This method does not find objects fainter than the single-pass limit. Reaching them would take stacking the passes with a shift along trial velocities, which this method does not do.
  • Known asteroids in the field at the time of each exposure come from the SkyBoT service (IMCCE) or JPL Horizons: a track that is found can be labeled right away.

Second example: ε Indi B

Blind search: 140 sources, 135 stationary, two tracks. No. 2 is 4.52″/yr toward 128°; according to Gaia, ε Indi B is at this place, 4.58″/yr toward 126°, and the positions differ by 0.6–0.7″. No. 1 is the bright ε Indi A, 6.7′ away from it. It is saturated, so its speed came out rough: 5.88″/yr toward 127° against the catalog 4.71″/yr toward 123°. The search itself showed that the two stars move across the sky together. Before the saturated-zone fix, the flat top of ε Indi A produced more than two thousand false tracks here.

sections.title: The anomaly map (in the lab)
sections.html:
Which sources of a field do not have the spectrum of an ordinary star of that field? (Service: /api/field_anomaly, engine/anomaly.py, the port of anomaly.py; a background job on a finished field, started by a button because it reads every exposure.)

  • Sources. The sources that stand still in the search between passes at S/N 12 or more (the brightest 300, saturated ones left out) and every track, measured where the track puts it. Each is measured in every exposure of the field (at most 800) with the PSF photometry of a clicked object, the OUTLIER flag kept for tracks; the windows are the field's own, so the reads come from its cache.
  • Comparison. The points of a source are binned into 24 wavelength bins (median, error from the spread); a source needs 60 points and 20 bins. The shape is the fluxes over their sum. The “ordinary star” is the median shape of the field plus two principal components of the bulk of the sources (temperature and reddening move a stellar spectrum along them); every source is fitted with that family and its anomaly is the rms of what is left in units of its error (the model adds a 5 % floor). A source is anomalous when its anomaly is beyond the median of the field by 6 robust sigma. With fewer than 12 sources with a spectrum the job says that no ordinary star can be defined.
  • Drawn. Rings only above the threshold; a click opens a card with the number, the S/N and the binned spectrum over the fit of the ordinary star, and the full spectrum on the Spectrum tab. It is a lead, not a finding: a blend, a variable star or a bad detector can do it too.

On ε Indi, RA 331.077 Dec −56.794, 20′ (595 exposures, 65 sources compared): the median anomaly of the field is 0.48 (robust scatter 0.15), the threshold 1.38 and 6 sources are above it. The strongest, by a wide margin (11.8, the next is 3.0), is the track of the brown dwarf ε Indi B (4.5″/yr, S/N 260): its spectrum has the peaks at 1.3, 1.6, 2.1 and 4 µm that no ordinary star has. The other five (3.0 to 1.6) are not explained here.

Limits. A 5′ field has about seven sources: no ordinary star can be defined, the job says so. The five weaker ones are leads that nobody has checked against catalogues. The family is two principal components of the field itself: a field of only one kind of star (a cluster) has a narrow bulk and flags more.

sections.title: Find Planet X in the lab: the distance slider (one pass)
sections.html:
A body beyond Neptune is too faint for one frame and does not stand still: the telescope rides the Earth around the Sun, so the body slides across the sky by parallax (the farther, the less) plus its own slow motion. In the lab, with a field of at most 20′ open, the button Look for distant bodies here starts the job /api/field_distant (engine/distant.py, the port of px.py) for one pass (the pass on show; the field is cut to 18′ at 20′).

  • Products. Every exposure of D1–D3 of every pass of the field on a grid of 3.075″, background removed (ZODI, then the median in 40 wavelength bins), OUTLIER kept, smoothed to a point source; the exposures of a visit combined by their median; the static sky of a detector is the clipped mean of its visits in all the other passes; stars of the static sky are masked with a margin that grows with their brightness; difference = visit − static sky, clipped at ±5σ.
  • The scan. A hypothesis is a distance (30–300 au) and an own motion (up to the escape speed); the telescope’s position in every visit (Earth from ERFA plus the spacecraft) gives the parallax offsets; the differences are shifted and added with weights 1/σ², the S/N is scaled by the sum’s own robust spread. Per sky point the best S/N and its hypothesis are kept; the same on the negated differences gives the height that noise alone reaches, and a peak counts only above 1.05 times that. The position and the own motion of each peak are then tuned on the unclipped differences; its distance comes as an interval (where the S/N is within 1 of the best), because a short arc trades the distance against the own motion. The scan is capped at a million hypotheses (about 13 minutes); a nearer minimum distance means many more.
  • Photometry. PSF photometry in every exposure of the pass at the place the track gives, minus the same sky places in the exposures of the other passes (the five nearest in wavelength, same detector); the same on four control tracks 1′ aside. Confirmed: photometry ≥ 5σ and a positive flux in every detector with four points or more and a path of at least 12″ over the pass.
  • The slider. The browser receives the differences of the visits (a byte each) and the offsets of every visit for 48 distances, shifts them by the chosen distance and own motion and adds them (on the CPU, not in a shader): a point comes into focus at the body’s distance and smears beyond it. “Show the noise” does the same on the negated differences. Nothing is marked; the peaks of the scan are listed and a click puts the sliders on one.

Eris (RA 27.378, Dec −0.120, 18′, the pass of July 2025; D1–D3, 315 exposures of 3 passes, 18 visits in the pass, 3.6 × 10⁵ hypotheses, a scan of 274 s on 6 threads while the service stays responsive: the health answer took under 4 ms): found blind, 12.0σ against a ceiling of 6.7σ, 96.4 au (52–182), 2″ from the JPL position; photometry 0.072 ± 0.008 mJy, 8.7σ (D1 0.131, D2 0.068, D3 0.040 mJy: it falls with wavelength, the icy colour), control tracks 2.1, 0.6, 0.2, −0.6σ (none reaches 5). Offline: 11.5σ in the scan, about 0.10 mJy.

Limits. One search reaches about V 20–21 in reflected light; the predicted Planet Nine is fainter, and the one place SPHEREx adds to the existing searches is D4 near 3 µm (a margin of 1.4–1.7×), which is not a product of the lab yet. The distance of one pass is an interval of a factor of 3. Work in progress, not yet checked in the lab: the sum of all passes along one orbit (engine/deepsum.py, /api/field_deep, the block “Deep sum of the passes”: it plans first and shows the estimate of the time, the scan runs in six worker processes; the centres of the other passes are a guess from a circular prograde orbit and a body with another own motion can miss the field). Not built: the link of passes and the jump corridor, the WISE archive check, one card for the four kinds of finds. The photometry of the first run read 0.043 mJy until the place was refined; the flux now depends on that refinement.

sections.title: Verification and the orbit model (the search inside a pass)
sections.html:
The candidates of the film are checked and linked in the same service job (run_visits; engine/orbit.py is the port of orbit.py; the verification follows fast.verify).

  • On − off photometry. On: the PSF flux at the candidate's place in every exposure of its own visit (engine/photometry.py, the OUTLIER flag is not a defect here: the pipeline puts it on moving bodies). Off: the median of the nine nearest in wavelength (within 12 %) of the fluxes at the same place in the exposures of the same detector at least 0.2 d from the visit, taken from every pass of the field (a star is where it was). Stage 1 measures at the detection place (known to about a grid pixel); a candidate that is positive in every exposure of its visit and at 2σ is measured again with the place free within 0.6 pixel in every exposure, the references at the fitted place. The windows of the field are read without VARIANCE, so the noise of an exposure is its robust scatter. A control measures the same 40″ to the side of every eighth candidate: its significances scatter around 0 (−1.7 to +0.7 on the field below), none passes.
  • The orbit model. A straight line is wrong over days: the Earth carries the telescope (30 km/s) and the telescope circles the Earth (±5″ at 2 au, different in every visit). A body on a two-body heliocentric orbit is seen from the observer (Earth by ERFA epv00 plus the spacecraft position X_SC, Y_SC, Z_SC of the exposures); two sky places and the distances at them fix the orbit (a grid uniform in 1/distance from 0.4 to 6 au, orbits with e < 0.6 and a between 0.8 and 8 au), and one hypothesis must explain all members within 5″. Candidates that are positive in every exposure and at 2σ are linked; a track must then reach 5σ together (the sum of its members' significances over the square root of their number). The visits where the body was not found are looked at on the motion maps at the place the orbit predicts (≥ 3.5σ within 1.5 pixel). The scrambled control moves the linked candidates to chance places and counts the tracks chance makes; only tracks longer than what chance makes (fewer than 0.15 per field) are drawn. A track gets its distance and its range.

On the ecliptic field RA 169.8917, Dec +4.3514, 20′, the pass of December 2025: 57 candidates, 52 with enough references, 8 verified by themselves at 4σ (the control: 0 of 8 places aside), 22 linkable (positive and ≥ 2σ). (9078) 1994 PB2 is linked by the orbit through 3 visits: residual 0.37″ (the straight line left 0.71″), 9.2σ together, distance 3.5 au (2.2–3.5), SkyBoT names it. The control on the 22 linked candidates made 0 chance tracks through three visits in 12 trials.

Limits. Orwell is not linked: its three candidates have 5.8σ, 3.6σ and 2.0σ, and the last is under the 2σ bar for linking. Lowering the bar to 1σ links more candidates (27) and chance then makes 0.17 three-visit tracks per field, above the 0.15 allowed, so the three-visit tracks (PB2 among them) would not be drawn: the faint ones cannot be had at this depth without more false tracks. The control only moves candidates (it does not re-measure photometry at chance places), and a distance from three visits over 34 hours is a range, not a measurement. The recovery by flux in the visits where a body was not found is done on the motion maps, not on the exposures.

sections.title: The film of one pass: bodies that cross the field in days
sections.html:
A body that crosses the field in days, an asteroid, is in no picture of the passes: at every place it is seen in one visit of a few exposures out of a pass of many visits, and the stack of the pass averages it away. The film shows the visits of one pass one after another, in time order, so that a person can see such a body hop across the field. The lab makes it when a field is opened (from the windows the field job has already read), for the pass with the most exposures of detectors D1–D3; the other passes are a click away.

How a frame is made

  • Every exposure of the pass is put on its own on a grid of at most 400 points across the field (3.075″ or coarser), smoothed to the size of a point source (3.2″), with the background removed as for the stacks and the pixels flagged OUTLIER kept: the SPHEREx pipeline puts that flag on moving bodies.
  • A visit is the exposures of one detector taken less than half an hour apart. Its frame is the median of its exposures at every place: a cosmic-ray hit is in one exposure and drops out, a body is in all of them and stays. Visits with at least three exposures are used where most visits have them; a visit that covers less than half of the field is left out, because its frame would be mostly empty.
  • The frames of one detector are aligned on their bright sources (cross-correlation with their median, a parabola through the peak, at most two grid points): a residual shift of a few tenths of a point leaves every star as a bright-dark pair.
  • Motion only: the frame minus the median of the frames of the same detector in the pass (the static sky), divided by the robust scatter of that difference. The places where the static sky shows a source above 4σ, grown by two grid points, are masked and drawn dim grey: an undersampled star never subtracts cleanly. On the screen a place is dark below 3.5σ and bright amber from about 7σ, and a bright point is spread over its 3 × 3 neighbours so that it is big enough to see; this is a display aid and changes no value. Sky shows the frame itself.

What the search adds, and how far it can be trusted

  • Candidates are the peaks of the motion maps of at least 6σ outside the mask, brighter than 0.74 of what the static sky shows there. At 5σ the maps hold about ten times more noise peaks, and chance makes dozens of three-visit tracks per field.
  • Candidates of different visits are linked along straight lines of 3–200″ per hour within 4″; a track is kept when its scatter about the line is at most 1.5″. Its other visits inside its time span (± half a day) are recovered on the motion maps: a visit counts when the map is at least 3.5σ within 1.5 grid points of the predicted place.
  • Control: the same candidates are moved to chance places (their times and visits kept), linked and recovered in exactly the same way, 20 times. A track is drawn only when chance makes fewer than 0.15 tracks of its length per field. Every track drawn is checked against IMCCE SkyBoT afterwards (a known body within 30″ at its middle visit, moving within 40 % of its rate); a track with no known body is called a lead, not a discovery.

The test: one pass of the field near the ecliptic

RA 169.8917°, Dec +4.3514°, 20′, the pass of 2–20 December 2025, opened by coordinates only: 131 exposures of D1–D3 make 24 frames (4 visits that cover less than half of the field left out); 57 candidates; chance makes 0.05 three-visit tracks per field. The search found one track, 21.8″ per hour through three visits, scatter 0.7″; the check afterwards names it (9078) 1994 PB2, V 18.9, 3.5″ from the SkyBoT position. In the motion-only film the body is the brightest point of four consecutive frames, and (11020) Orwell, V 18.8, is as clear in three later frames. The pictures: docs/evidence/stage5/film_ecliptic_*.jpg.

Limits. The candidates are not yet verified by photometry on the exposures (the on − off check of the offline pipeline), and the tracks are straight lines: Orwell is not linked because its path over a day and a half bends more than 4″ (the Earth carries the telescope; the orbit model of the offline search handles it). The fourth visit of (9078) falls on a masked static source. Bodies fainter than about V 19 give one or two candidates and are not linked; in the film they can still be seen by eye in some frames. The film is made from the exposures that overlap the field, so its time sampling is the survey's: a few visits a day, gaps of days.

sections.title: Objects that cross the field in days: spectrum along a track, blind search
sections.html:
Known asteroids passed through the field of Barnard's Star during the observations. They are not in any super-frame, but their flux can be measured at the place where the object was at the moment of each exposure.

The test and its result

The JPL service returns the known small bodies for a given time and field of view. During the observations five asteroids brighter than V = 19.5 passed near the field. Three fell in the cutouts; two of them in enough exposures: (4008) Corbin (26 exposures, August 21–25, 2025) and (15101) 2000 AY150 (20 exposures, March 15, 2026). Both are V = 18.1.

SPHEREx observes in visits: four exposures two minutes apart, the next visit hours or days later. Within a visit an asteroid shifts by less than a pixel, between visits by arcminutes. That is why it is not in the super-frame: at each place it is seen in four exposures out of twenty.

ObjectDetector, µmFramesFlux, mJy
(4008) CorbinD2, 1.1–1.690.36 ± 0.01
D3, 2.0–2.140.33 ± 0.04
D5, 3.8–4.390.14 ± 0.03
D6, 4.7–4.840.14 ± 0.06
(15101) 2000 AY150D2, 1.2–1.6100.26 ± 0.02
D5, 3.9–4.3100.48 ± 0.07

Control: the same procedure 60–90″ to the side along the track, where there is no object, gives −0.00 ± 0.01 mJy in D2 for both, and −0.01 ± 0.01 and −0.02 ± 0.01 mJy in D5. A single exposure in D2 gives a signal 3–11 times its error, in D5–D6 from zero to 7 times; that is why the table lists averages per detector.

The spectra differ. For Corbin the flux at 4 µm is 2.6 times lower than at 1.3 µm. For 2000 AY150 it is 1.9 times higher. This is how an asteroid's own thermal emission on top of reflected sunlight should look; Corbin, according to JPL, has a high albedo (0.26), and it is farther from the Sun. This agrees with the expectation, but with two to four detectors per object it is an observation, not a proof.

The same technique on Barnard's Star itself: if its halo is measured along the Gaia track, the scatter of the points in D4–D6 is 2–4%; if at the fixed coordinates of the first pass, it is 16–21%.

The spectrum of a moving object can be measured along the track even when the object is not visible in any single image.

Blind search: what works and what does not

The task: find such objects knowing nothing about them. A search on single-exposure detections alone drowns: about a thousand false detections per exposure and 11 thousand candidates. So every candidate is verified by the same measurement that is used for a known asteroid: the flux in the visit minus the flux at the same place on the sky on other days.

# candidates: peaks of the PSF filter in (exposure − the rest), detectors D1–D3, S/N ≥ 5
# visit = 4 exposures 2 minutes apart; visit candidate: detections within 7″ in ≥ 3 exposures
for c in visit_candidates:
    on  = [psf_flux(exp, c.pos[exp]) for exp in visit]
    off = median(psf_flux(r, c.pos) for r in the 9 exposures nearest in λ
                 of the same detector from other days)
    d = on - off;  sig = mean(d) / sqrt(std(d)**2 / n + err_off**2)
    # step 1: positions as is; those with all d > 0 and sig ≥ 1 go on
    # step 2: the position is free within ±0.6 pixel (amplitude positive only),
    #         off is measured at the found position, now with no freedom; accepted if sig ≥ 5
    # halo rule: 0.6 * flux / 0.889 > 3 * halo_level
# noise control: the same two steps 40″ to the side of the candidate
# track: verified sources of ≥ 3 visits on a straight line, 3–200″/h
#   (later the straight line was replaced by an orbit: see the field near the ecliptic below)

The field of Barnard's Star: of 11,430 candidates 32 passed verification, 27 of them outside the halos of bright stars. At the control positions 1 of 1547 passed verification, so noise accounts for about seven of the 32. Corbin was found blind in one visit: 0.32 mJy, 17σ, 1″ from the ephemeris. 2000 AY150 in its visit gave 0.26 mJy and 4.4σ against a threshold of 5σ and did not pass. The other visits of both asteroids did not make it into the candidates: they have fewer than three detections.

After the search JPL was asked about all 32 places and times. An answer came for 23: a known asteroid (down to V = 23) stands behind only one of them, and it is Corbin. What the rest are is not known: some are noise, some lie at the very edge of the field.

The field of ε Indi: of 1432 candidates 7 passed, 3 of them outside the halo of ε Indi A; in the control, 0 of 275. There are no known asteroids in the cutouts of this field, so there is nothing to compare against.

There are no tracks through three visits in these two fields: each asteroid gives at most one verified visit. Track linking was tested on a separate field near the ecliptic, where there are many asteroids: the result is below.

The visit-level search that worked near the ecliptic was also repeated on the field of Barnard's Star. It gave no more than before: 30,050 candidates in 36 visits, 115 passed verification, 111 of them outside halos; at the control positions 6 of 5048, so about 30 of the 115 are noise. Corbin is verified in one visit of the three where it made it into the candidates; 2000 AY150 made it into the candidates in one visit and did not pass verification. There are no tracks. The field is dense: a star lies under almost every point of the path, and the “visit minus the rest” difference is noisier there. Linking with a motion model gave one triple of visits there, and it did not pass the orbit check: 0.6σ over six visits. On scrambled sources there are 0.9 such triples per trial.

How it is done

# 1. who was in the field: JPL Small-Body Identification, one request per visit
GET https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/sb_ident.api?sb-kind=a&mpc-code=500&two-pass=true
    &obs-time=2025-08-24_11:47:25&fov-ra-center=17-57-47&fov-dec-center=04-46-07
    &fov-ra-hwidth=0.7&fov-dec-hwidth=0.7&vmag-lim=19.5&mag-required=true
# 2. where the object was at the moment of each exposure: JPL Horizons, the observer is SPHEREx itself
GET https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api?COMMAND='4008;'&CENTER='500@-163182'
    &EPHEM_TYPE='OBSERVER'&TLIST_TYPE='MJD'&TLIST='60911.508' ...&QUANTITIES='1,3,9,19,20,24'
# 3. the flux in each exposure
on   = psf_flux(exp, ra_t, dec_t)                     # PSF fit, as for a star
refs = exposures of the same detector on other days, the 9 nearest in wavelength
off  = median(psf_flux(r, ra_t, dec_t) for r in refs) # starlight under the object
flux = on - off
# 4. control: the same at positions shifted along the track by ±60″ and ±90″
  • The observer in the ephemeris is the spacecraft, not the center of the Earth. SPHEREx flies in a low orbit, and for these asteroids the difference was 1.1–2.6″, up to 40% of a pixel.
  • Subtracting off is mandatory: the field is crowded, and a faint star almost always lies under the track. Without it Corbin in D3 comes out at 0.45 mJy instead of 0.33.
  • The image for such an object is the median of the exposures in a box that travels with it (bottom left in the video). A star stays at one place in the box only during one visit and fades in the median; the object stays at the center.
  • A request to the identification service takes 20–30 seconds. It has to run in the background and be cached by field and date.
  • For an object without a known orbit (Planet X) there is no ephemeris. Then the track is taken from the search over super-frames, as in the search between passes, and within a pass the parallactic shift is added.
  • Code: audit/ephem.py (ephemerides), mover.py (fluxes and control), vids_h.py (the video), fast.py, fastv.py and orbit.py (the blind search).

Field near the ecliptic: four tracks, four known asteroids

Testing track linking needs a field with many asteroids. We took a square degree on the ecliptic far from the Milky Way (RA 169.89°, Dec +4.35°) and one pass: December 14–20, 2025, 121 exposures. According to JPL, 26 known asteroids brighter than V = 20.5 fell into the cutouts during that week, seven of them no fainter than V = 19.

The single-exposure search described above finds nothing in this field: not a single candidate near the known asteroids. There are three reasons.

  • The OUTLIER flag. The SPHEREx pipeline itself marks the pixels of an asteroid as outliers. Within a pixel of the ephemeris the flag is set in 143 exposures out of 199 (72%); at random positions, in 18%. A mask or a PSF fit that drops flagged pixels erases the asteroid. For a search for moving objects these pixels must be kept.
  • Single-exposure threshold. An asteroid of V = 18 gives 6–8σ in one exposure, V = 19 gives 3–4σ. Only the brightest pass the condition “5σ in three exposures of a visit”. Within a visit an asteroid shifts by less than a pixel, so the exposures of a visit can be stacked first.
  • Large pixel. The same object falls into different pixels in the four exposures of a visit, and the median of unsmoothed images loses it. Each exposure must first be smoothed to the size of a point source.

After these fixes: 2857 candidates in 11 visits of D2 and D3, 94 passed verification, 0 of 663 at the control positions.

Straight-line linking gave three tracks. It did not link the fourth bright asteroid, (11020) Orwell: its three verified visits do not lie on a straight line, the middle one is 19″ away from it with a tolerance of 8″. This is not noise. The telescope itself moves along a curve: the Earth carries it around the Sun. According to the JPL ephemerides, for 14 asteroids of this field the path on the sky departs from a straight line by 15–61″ over 3–5 days. The spacecraft's orbit around the Earth adds no more than 1.1″ to this.

Linking with a motion model. A track is an orbit around the Sun seen from the moving telescope. Where the telescope is, is known: the position of the Earth comes from the ephemeris built into astropy, and the position of the spacecraft relative to the center of the Earth is written in the header of every frame. Two quantities are unknown: the distance to the object and the rate at which it changes. They are scanned on a grid. If the distances from JPL are put into the model, it reproduces the JPL ephemerides to better than 0.01″.

The model linked six chains: the three found with a straight line and three triples of visits. For a triple, linking alone is not enough: on scrambled sources, random triples come out at 3.5 per trial. So a triple is checked once more. The orbit says where the object was in the other visits, and the flux is measured there. One triple has flux in all four visits where it can be measured: this is (11020) Orwell. The other two have no flux and were discarded.

No.VisitsOverSpeedFluxResidual: straight line → orbitDistance, auPer JPLTo the ephemeris
1768 h32.5″/h0.27–0.37 mJy6.8″ → 1.8″2.46 (1.80–2.52)(9952) 1991 AK, V = 18.1; 2.28 au1.0–3.1″
2570 h35.6″/h0.13–0.32 mJy9.5″ → 1.0″2.17 (1.90–2.24)(43959) 1997 CB26, V = 18.4; 1.98 au0.7–2.1″
