“3 + 4” means three visits where the search found the object and four more where its flux was measured at the place given by the orbit. The orbit passes through three points exactly; it has no residual. The numbers are the same as in the image.

  • There are no false tracks. Control on scrambled sources, 100 trials: random triples average 3.5 per trial, a quadruple occurs in 1% of trials, there are no quintuples. None of the 48 random triples passed the orbit check: their combined flux significance has a median of 0 and is no more than 1.4σ, with a threshold of 5σ.
  • (11020) Orwell in the four additional visits: 0.10–0.15 mJy, 3.0–4.4σ in each, 7.1σ together. (9078) gained two visits in the same way: 4.3 and 4.4σ. The place given by the orbit in these visits differs from the JPL ephemeris by 0.3–1.6″.
  • The residual from the orbit for the three long tracks is 1.0–1.9″; from a straight line it was 5.8–9.5″. The linking tolerance was therefore lowered from 8″ to 5″.
  • The distance comes from the bend of the path: the closer the object, the stronger the bend. The error against JPL is 4–13%, and all four JPL values lie inside the fit interval. The interval is wide, 16–36% of the distance itself: over three days the distance and its rate of change act on the path almost identically. Orbital elements cannot be determined from such an arc.
  • The orbit check is done only in those visits where all the orbits that fit agree within 3″. One to three days beyond the end of the arc they diverge by 5–26″, and such visits are not measured.
  • For (43959), the flux in the only additional visit came out negative: −0.13 ± 0.05 mJy, although the place given by the orbit is only 1.3″ from the ephemeris. This is not explained.
  • Allowed orbits have a semi-major axis of 0.8–8 au and an eccentricity up to 0.6, at a distance of 0.4–6 au from the telescope. This linking will not link a comet on a parabola or an object farther than 6 au.
  • Of the 94 verified sources, 25 sit on eight known asteroids. The other 69 are faint (about 0.1 mJy, 5–6σ) and look like noise at the threshold: the search and the verification look at the same pixels. They did not link into tracks.
  • There are no tracks fainter than V = 19: for such asteroids one or two visits are verified.
  • D1 did not go into the search: all its visits fit within three hours, so there is nothing to compare with. The brightest asteroid of the week, (1737) Severny, V = 16.6, was in the field only in the last visit, right at the edge, and did not make it into the candidates.
  • The JPL list is not fed into the search: the comparison is made against the finished tracks.
  • The list of exposures of this field was built without the IRSA query service, which did not respond at the time: from the open copy of the archive in the cloud, where the file headers are read with partial downloads and show which frames cover the field. The cutouts themselves came from IRSA.

What was found

Stack of the field over the pass. Colored lines are tracks found blind. Colored circles are visits where the search found the object; diamonds are visits where its flux was measured at the place given by the orbit. Gray circles are verified sources of a single visit. Thin gray lines are the paths of known asteroids per JPL.

How it is computed

# fastv.py: candidates are taken per visit, not per exposure
for exp in D2, D3:                                 # pixels with the OUTLIER flag stay
    g[exp] = gauss(splat(exp), 3.2″)               # size of a point source
for visit:                                         # a visit: at least three exposures
    vis[visit] = median(g[exp] for exp in visit)   # a cosmic-ray hit is in one and drops out
ref  = median(vis over detector visits in pass)    # static sky
d    = vis[visit] - ref
sn   = (d - median(d)) / (1.4826 * MAD(d))
cand = local_max(sn) & (sn >= 5) & (d >= 0.74 * ref)
# verification of each candidate: on − off per exposure, as before,
# but the OUTLIER flag is not masked in the PSF fit either
# orbit.py: a track is one orbit around the Sun seen from the telescope
obs[visit] = earth(t) + (X_SC, Y_SC, Z_SC)   # Earth: erfa.epv00; spacecraft: header
for (i, j) in pairs of sources from different visits, 3–200″/h:
    for D in 0.4…6 au (step 0.04 in 1/D), dD in −48…48 km/s (step 4):
        X_i = obs_i + D * n_i;  X_j = obs_j + (D + dD * T) * n_j
        V_i = velocity of the Kepler orbit that leads from X_i to X_j in time T
        if not (0.8 < a < 8 au and e < 0.6): continue
        pred[visit] = direction(kepler(X_i, V_i, t_visit) - obs[visit])
    # between grid nodes pred is interpolated linearly, down to a step of 1.7″
    members = sources of other visits closer than 5″ to pred under ONE hypothesis
# group fit: for each hypothesis, subtract from (measured − pred)
#   a straight line in time — the error of the two anchor points; the residual is the measure
#   a member farther than 10″ is dropped; a source belongs to one track
# orbit check: on − off where the orbit puts the object in the other
#   visits (if the orbits that fit agree within 3″);  Z = sum(d / err) / sqrt(n)
# accepted: ≥ 4 visits, or 3 visits and Z ≥ 5 over at least two others
# control: the same after scrambling the sources, 100 times
  • A detector is taken into the search only if its visits have at least five exposures of other visits no closer than 0.2 days: otherwise there is nothing to measure the “sky without the object” with.
  • A visit is stacked with the median, not the mean: a cosmic-ray hit is in one exposure out of four and does not get into the median. Single-exposure rejection is not applied here: it takes a bright fast object for a hit.
  • The motion model needs only the frame headers and the Earth ephemeris from astropy. No network is needed, and no information about the objects is fed into it.
  • Scanning the hypotheses replaces orbit fitting: a pair of sources and one hypothesis define the orbit completely, and it remains to compare it with the other visits. 94 sources take 11 seconds.
  • Code: fastv.py (candidates per visit, orbit check), fast.py (on − off photometry), orbit.py (motion model, linking, control), fast_fig.py (the image); ecl/ — how the field was assembled.

Second example: ε Indi B

There is no separate video: it is the video of the ε Indi B spectrum above. The gray circles in it are the same exposures measured at the fixed coordinates of the first pass. In October 2025 the object had moved 2″ away from them, and about 80% of the flux remains. In September 2026 it had moved 6.5″ away, and 6 to 17% remains. For an object that shifts by a pixel per year, a spectrum without a track simply disappears.

sections.title: Find Planet X: adding the exposures along the motion
sections.html:
A search for slow, faint bodies of the outer Solar System: the “distance knob” inside one pass, the “jump” between passes, and the sum of all passes along one orbit.

3 of 3passes in which Eris and Makemake were found blind
0.5%largest difference between our distance and JPL
45″, 57″error of the predicted place in the third pass
0 of 64control tracks that reached 5σ
0.02–0.07 mJy5σ depth of one pass along a known track
V ≈ 19–20blind limit of one pass, depending on the color of the body
9.1σSedna, V = 20.8, found blind in the sum of three passes
1.4–1.7×deeper than the WISE search for Planet Nine at 3 µm, measured
0 confirmedone candidate at 394 au, ruled out with ten years of WISE images

The challenge asks for a tool that makes moving objects easy to spot, “even new planets”. Things in the sky move in three different ways, and each needs its own search. The first two are the searches of the previous sections. This section and the next ones are about the third.

What movesHow it looks in SPHEREx dataSearch
Nearby stars, brown dwarfsarcseconds per year: a shift between passes, the object is in every stackcompare the stacks of the passes
Asteroids, cometsarcminutes per day: in a new place in every visit, in no stack at allcandidates per visit, linked by an orbit inside one pass
Find Planet Xa few arcseconds per day inside a pass, a jump of tens of arcminutes between passes; too faint for one exposureadd the exposures along the motion (this section)

The jump has a simple cause. SPHEREx looks at a place of the sky when it is 90° from the Sun. Half a year later it looks at the same place from the other side of the Earth's orbit, 2 au away. A body at distance d is then seen displaced by about 2 au / d: 72′ at 95 au, 14′ at 500 au. Stars do not jump, so the size of the jump is the distance.

1. Focusing on a track

Eris, V = 18.7, pass of January 2026. The twelve visits are added along a growing share of the track the search found. With no shift the body is smeared over 190″ and the sum shows nothing; at 100% it gathers into a point of 14σ, twice the height the noise reaches.

2. The jump between passes

The detection of July 2025 is carried half a year forward for an assumed distance. The predicted place slides across the January field by 53″ per astronomical unit. The body found blind in January lies 267″ from the line, at the 86 au mark: one pass alone gives the distance to about 10%. One orbit through both tracks then gives 95.6 ± 1.0 au; JPL says 95.4.

3. Sedna: the limit

Sedna, V = 20.8, three passes. The blind search of one pass does not find it; the sum of three passes does, see the third version below. Added along the JPL ephemeris, visit by visit, it grows to a clear detection, while the same sum on an empty track beside it stays at zero.

Eris in three passes

Left: the first pass, added as it is and along the track. The flat gray patch is a masked static source. Right: the three blind detections on the sky, the JPL path (drawn for comparison only) and the place predicted for the third pass from the first two.

Input: Level 2 cutouts of one field from at least two passes. Nothing about any body is given to the search. Detectors D1–D3 (0.75–2.4 µm) are used, because a cold body is seen in reflected sunlight; D4 can be added.

Inside one pass: the distance knob

  1. Put every exposure on a sky grid. Background: the ZODI extension, then the median in 40 wavelength bins (this removes the helium airglow stripe in D1), then a clipped median. Flagged pixels are dropped, except the OUTLIER flag: the SPHEREx pipeline puts it on moving bodies. Grid step 3.075″, half a pixel; each pixel is spread with a 1.85″ kernel and the image is smoothed to the size of a point source, 3.2″.
  2. Combine the exposures of a visit by a median. Near the ecliptic the exposures come in visits of four, two minutes apart; the median drops cosmic rays. Far from the ecliptic they come alone or in groups of two to four. Groups of three or more get a median, of a pair the lower value is taken, and in a single exposure the points more than 5σ off are left out.
  3. Subtract the static sky. Static sky = mean of the visits of the same detector from all other passes, when the body was elsewhere; values 3σ off the median are left out of the mean. Difference = visit − static sky, clipped at ±5σ so that one bad visit cannot make a detection.
  4. Mask what the static sky shows. Every grid point where the static sky is above 4σ is masked, with a margin that grows with the brightness of the source: two grid points at 4σ, ten at 4000σ. A SPHEREx pixel is larger than a star image, so a star never subtracts cleanly; its residual is the same in every visit and would add up. Without the mask the noise reached 17σ; with a fixed margin of two points the strongest false peaks sat 3–19″ from the brightest stars. The mask costs 19–25% of the field.
  5. Scan the hypotheses. A hypothesis is a heliocentric distance d and an own motion μ. A point at distance d on the line of sight is seen from the position of the telescope in every visit: that is the parallax path. Earth comes from ERFA (built into astropy), the spacecraft from the header keywords X_SC, Y_SC, Z_SC. The own motion is added as μ·(t − t0) and is limited by the escape speed, 5016″/day / d1.5. The grid is uniform in 1/d and in μ, so that neighboring hypotheses differ by at most 3″ in any visit.
  6. Add along each hypothesis. The differences are shifted and added with weights 1/σ²; the result is divided by the square root of the summed weights and then by the robust spread of the sum itself. The second division is needed because the noise of the static sky is common to the visits of a detector: the formal error was 3–26% too low. For every sky point the best signal-to-noise ratio and its hypothesis are kept.
  7. Let the noise set the threshold. The same sums of the negated differences give the height that noise alone reaches with this many hypotheses: 6.5–9σ in our fields. Candidates are the peaks more than 5% above that height. A body leaves a ridge of weaker peaks along its track; they are dropped.
  8. Tune bright candidates. A bright body is clipped in every visit, so many hypotheses give the same sum. For such candidates the place and μ are tuned on the unclipped differences, with the visit images read at fractional positions.
  9. Check on the exposures. Along the track of the candidate, the PSF flux is measured in every exposure of the pass. From each value the median flux at the same sky place in the five exposures of the other pass nearest in wavelength is subtracted. Accepted if the weighted mean is at least 5σ, every detector is positive, and the track is longer than 12″.
  10. Control. The same measurement on four tracks one arcminute aside. None of 64 such tracks reached 5σ.

Between passes: the jump

  1. Take three points from every candidate track: the first, middle and last visit of its pass.
  2. Fit one orbit through the tracks of two passes. Six free numbers: the two end points of the whole arc, the distance at the first point, and its rate of change. The orbit is a two-body orbit around the Sun, seen from the telescope. The speed is kept below the escape speed: two passes do not fix the motion along the line of sight, and without this the fit drifts to an open orbit.
  3. One body or not. If the misfit is below 6″ and the orbit is closed, the two candidates are one body, and the fit gives its distance.
  4. Test on a third pass. The orbit predicts the place in the third pass. A candidate found there within 2′ confirms the body, and all three passes are fitted together.

Two more rules

  • Does it move. A candidate that shifts by less than two pixels over the pass is a sky place that was brighter in this pass than in the others: a variable star or a flare. It is reported as a change of brightness, not as a body.
  • From one pass the distance is weak. Over two weeks the parallax shift and the own motion act on the track in almost the same way. Eris fits anything from 50 to 170 au in one pass. The knob becomes sharp only with the jump.

Parameters

ParameterValueWhy
grid step3.075″half a SPHEREx pixel
clip of a visit difference±5σone visit cannot decide
mask of the static skyabove 4σ; margin 2 to 10 points, by brightnessstar residuals add up, wings of bright stars reach far
static skymean over all other passes, 3σ clipless noisy than a median of one pass
scale of the sumits own robust spreadthe static-sky noise is shared by the visits
step between hypotheses3″ in any visitone grid point
largest own motion5016″/day / d1.5escape speed at d au
coverage of a sumat least 60% of the weightno sums from a few visits
threshold1.05 × noise ceiling, at least 5σthe noise is not Gaussian
photometry≥ 5σ, all detectors positiveindependent of the sum
shortest track of a body12″ over the passtwo pixels; less is a static change
link of two passesmisfit ≤ 6″, closed orbitposition error of a track is 2–3″

Pseudo-code

# px.py: one pass of one field
for visit in pass:                                      # a visit = median of its exposures
    diff[visit] = clip(visit - clipped_mean(visits of the same detector in all other passes), ±5σ)
    diff[visit][static_sky > 4σ, margin 2..10 points by brightness] = no data
obs[visit] = earth(t) + (X_SC, Y_SC, Z_SC)              # Earth: erfa.epv00; spacecraft: header
for d in grid uniform in 1/d:                           # shift between neighbors ≤ 3″
    X0 = point on the line of sight at heliocentric distance d
    P[visit] = direction(X0 - obs[visit])               # the parallax path, exact
    for mu in disk |mu| ≤ 5016″/day / d**1.5:           # step 3″ per half pass
        off  = P + mu * (t - t0)
        sn   = sum(w * diff(x + off)) / sqrt(sum(w))    # w = 1/σ²
        sn  /= robust_spread(sn)                        # the static-sky noise is shared
        best = max(best, sn);  null = max(null, -sn)
cand = peaks of best above 1.05 * max(null), not below 5σ
for c in cand:
    if c is bright: tune place and mu on the unclipped differences
    on  = [psf_flux(exp, track(c, exp)) for exp in pass]
    off = [median(psf_flux(r, same sky place) for r in 5 nearest-in-wavelength exposures of another pass)]
    c.ok = mean(on - off) ≥ 5σ and every detector > 0 and track length ≥ 12″
# link.py: candidates of two passes
orbit = two-body orbit around the Sun through both tracks       # 6 parameters, speed below escape
same body if misfit ≤ 6″;  distance = orbit.distance
third pass: orbit.predict(t3) must land within 2′ of a candidate found there

  • Both bodies were found blind in each of the three passes, with tracks within a few arcseconds of JPL. The largest offset, 12.9″ for Makemake, is at the ends of a 37-day pass, outside the visits that entered the sum.
  • There are no false confirmations. Six more peaks rose above the noise ceiling in these fields; none passed the photometry. None of the 48 control tracks reached 5σ.
  • The distances agree with JPL within 0.5%.
  • The shape of the orbit is not determined. The semi-major axis of Eris came out as 67, 275 and 82 au in three computations (the true value is about 68 au), for Makemake 49 au against about 45. One year of data fixes the distance but not the speed along the line of sight.

  • Along the JPL ephemeris there is one hypothesis, and the same exposures give a detection in every pass.
  • The errors here are measured, not formal: the spread of the same measurement on 40 empty tracks 45–150″ from the body. Formal errors are 1.2–1.6 times too small.
  • The Sedna passes were searched on a narrowed range of 60–150 au. The full range for a 25-day pass is five million hypotheses, about an hour.
  • In the first version, with one reference pass, the search found in the first Sedna field a source of 0.044 mJy that moved only 7″ over the pass: a static place that was brighter than in the reference pass. 2MASS has no source there; it is not identified. With two reference passes it is no longer above the ceiling.

The second version: three improvements and what they gave

After the first run three things were tried to push the blind limit toward V = 21. The result in one line: far fewer false peaks and an honest noise scale, but almost no gain in depth. Every number in these sections except the Makemake rows is from this second version.

What was changed

  1. Cleaner subtraction. The static sky is a clipped mean over all other passes instead of a median of one pass. The mask margin grows with the brightness of the source. The sum is scaled by its own spread. Far from the ecliptic, groups of exposures are combined and far-off points of single exposures are left out.
  2. Linking of faint peaks between passes (px/link_faint.py). Peaks down to 4σ are kept. The place and apparent motion of a peak are carried to the other pass for every distance; a peak there within 5′ that moves within 1.5″/day of the prediction is a partner. Partners are fitted with one closed orbit. Control: the same with the peaks of the later passes mirrored about the field center.
  3. Weights by spectrum. A matched filter by detector with the mean colors of Eris, Makemake and Sedna: D1 : D2 : D3 = 1 : 0.8 : 0.35.

What it means

  • The false peaks are gone. In the high-latitude field there are 60–75 times fewer peaks above 6σ, and the noise ceiling dropped in all nine passes.
  • The depth hardly moved. Once the noise is scaled honestly, the signal of a body drops by nearly the same factor as the ceiling. The blind limit improved by 5–25% in five passes of six and got worse in one. It stays at about 0.045–0.065 mJy.
  • Weights by spectrum gave nothing for icy bodies: 1.00–1.03 times on Eris and Sedna. They are left as an option, --template=icy.
  • Faint peaks cannot be linked by their motion. Sedna's own peaks are in the lists, 6–14″ from its place at 4.6–5.5σ, but their motions are wrong by 9–15″/day: at 5σ the sum finds a place, not a track. In the three Sedna fields 98 pairs passed the quick test and one got a closed orbit (4.8σ and 5.5σ, 124 au); it is 3.6′ from Sedna and has no partner in the third pass. In the IRAS/AKARI field nothing was linked. The control gave no links in either case.
  • The expected two- to threefold gain did not come. The gap between the blind limit and the known-track limit is not made by artifacts. It is the price of scanning thousands of tracks instead of one.
  • What could still add depth: adding the passes together along one orbit. That was done next, see the third version below.

sections.title: Find Planet X: adding the passes together (Sedna found blind)
sections.html:
The second version ended with one idea left: add the visits of all passes along one orbit. That is done here (px/multi.py), and it found Sedna blind. The search has two stages now, because the sum alone turned out not to be enough.

How it works

  1. A hypothesis is an orbit. A body stands at a sky point of the middle pass at its middle visit, at heliocentric distance d, with own motion μ. Its speed along the line of sight is taken as zero. The orbit is carried to every visit of every pass as a two-body orbit around the Sun and is seen from where the telescope was.
  2. Two levels keep it affordable. A coarse step of μ, 3″ over the length of a pass, fixes the shape of the track inside each pass, so the visits of each pass are added once per coarse step. Inside it μ is stepped finely, by 4.5″ of shift in the outer passes, and the three pass images are shifted and added.
  3. Only orbits that stay in the data are tried. An orbit must land inside the downloaded field of every pass.
  4. Stage 1, the sum. For every orbit the signal-to-noise ratio of the sum, scaled by its own spread. The best value per sky point is kept, and the same for the negated data.
  5. Stage 2, photometry of the strongest peaks. The 100 strongest peaks of the sum and the 100 strongest of the negated sum are measured. First place, distance and μ are tuned on the visit images read at fractional positions. Then the PSF flux is measured along the orbit in every exposure of all passes, minus the same sky place in the other passes. The flux of a negated peak is negated.
  6. The threshold comes from the negated peaks. A candidate must have positive flux in every pass and a combined photometric signal above 1.05 times the best that a negated peak reaches.
  7. One source, one candidate. A body that is clear in one pass also gives peaks at wrong distances: its track in that pass plus noise in the others. Peaks that share a track in any pass, within 20″, are one source, and only the strongest is kept.

Why the sum alone is not enough

  • The noise ceiling of the sum is high. In the Sedna fields the negated sum reaches 8.1σ. The highest peaks are leftovers of the static sky in one pass, lifted by the noise of the other two: among millions of orbits the other passes always offer a positive fluctuation.
  • Sedna gives 6.6σ in the sum, and 4.8, 3.1 and 4.2σ in the passes along that orbit. The per-pass values quoted before, 5.2, 4.3 and 5.5σ, were the best over the hypotheses near its place and were raised by that choice. The 8.7σ expected from them was too optimistic.
  • Photometry tells them apart. It is made in the exposures themselves, against the same sky place at the same wavelength. The leftovers give 1–6σ there, Sedna gives 9.1σ.

What “blind” means here

  • The three fields were centered where Sedna was in each pass, so the search knew the area, 18′ across. It did not know the place inside, the distance or the motion.
  • A search with no prior place needs the outer passes over a strip about 1° long for these distances, because the jump depends on the distance. That is ten times more data per field.
  • For the Planet Nine range one 1° field holds all three passes; that case was run on the IRAS/AKARI field below.

sections.title: Find Planet X: detector D4 alone, orbits like Planet Nine, artificial bodies, a candidate and the WISE archive
sections.html:
The third version ended with an estimate: a blind search in D4 alone should be about twice deeper than the WISE search for Planet Nine. Here it is run and measured. The answer is 1.7 times in clean sky and 1.4–1.5 times near the ecliptic, where the planet is expected. One weak candidate came out of it. The WISE archive did not confirm it: it is a false alarm.

What was done

  1. D4 alone in two 1° fields, three passes, 250–2000 au: the clean field at high latitude (59 exposures) and a field near the ecliptic at RA 60.71°, Dec +8.62°, ecliptic latitude −12°, inside the band where the planet is predicted (60 exposures).
  2. A prior on the orbit (--prior=5,30,0.4,0.9): only orbits like the predicted planet are tried. Prograde, inclination 5–30° to the ecliptic, speed across the line of sight 0.4–0.9 of the escape speed. An orbit of inclination i crosses ecliptic latitude b at an angle ψ to the ecliptic with cos ψ = cos i / cos b, so the prior fixes the direction of the own motion. A field at a latitude above 30° has no such orbits; the clean field at −58° is one of those.
  3. A test with artificial bodies (--inject). 30 point images, six at each of five fluxes from 0.02 to 0.075 mJy, are added to the exposures in memory. Each moves along a closed orbit at 350–900 au, with a speed along the line of sight that the search does not model. The sum is then read on the own orbit of each body.
  4. The artificial image is calibrated on real exposures (dbg/inj_check.py). Its width is set so that the PSF photometry used for real bodies returns the flux that was put in: ratio 0.999 for D4 and 1.000 for D1–D3. With a first guess of the width the photometry read 30% too much in D4.
  5. The limit is the larger of two fluxes: the one from which the sum of a body reaches the weakest peak that went to photometry, and the photometry threshold times the error of a track.

The artificial bodies are used for this one number. No picture or video in these sections contains them.

What the test showed besides the limit

  • The estimate was too optimistic, and so was the promise for the prior. “Twice deeper than WISE” became 1.7 and 1.4–1.5. The prior cut the orbits 12 times and the time of the sum 10 times, but improved the limit by 11%, which is 0.12 magnitude; The expectation was 30–100 times fewer orbits and 0.3 magnitude.
  • With one detector the mask costs bodies. A body is lost if in any of the three passes its place is covered by the mask of a static source: 8 of 30 artificial bodies near the ecliptic and 2 of 30 in the clean field. With several detectors the masks differ, and less is lost: 1 of 30 in the D1–D4 search.
  • Many artificial bodies in one field disturb each other when all orbits are scanned: a bright one leaves peaks at wrong distances that cross the places of faint ones, and the faint ones came out at 8σ whatever their flux. That is why each body is read on its own orbit.
  • The earlier estimate for the D1–D4 search held. In the clean field a body with the same flux in all four detectors reaches photometry from 0.019 mJy; the estimate from Sedna's ratio was 0.02.
  • Over a large area the threshold has to go up, because every field is one more chance for noise. We estimate another 15–20% of depth for a thousand fields; this is not measured.

The candidate, and how the WISE archive ruled it out

In the ecliptic field, with the prior, one peak passed the threshold: 6.7σ in the sum, 7.7σ in the photometry against a threshold of 7.0σ. Distance 394 au, own motion 0.57″/day.

  • With an honest error it is 6.1σ. The errors in the table come from 30 empty tracks beside the orbit (px/follow.py). Together the passes give 0.034 ± 0.006 mJy. The 7.7σ above uses formal errors, as the threshold does.
  • Against: the threshold. In the search over all orbits of the same field the negated peaks reach 7.5σ, so a 7.7σ peak is not rare there. It passes only because the prior lowers the threshold. Six searches have now been run with a threshold just above the best negated peak; one false pass among them is to be expected.
  • Against: the neighbors. CatWISE has a static source of W1 = 16.0, which is 0.13 mJy, 5″ from the place in the second pass, and a faint one 8″ from the place in the third. The first place has nothing within 11″. False peaks sat next to such sources before.
  • Against: the other detectors. Along the same orbit D1–D3 give 0.008 ± 0.004 mJy, 1.8σ. A body that reflects sunlight evenly would be about twice brighter there than in D4. D5 gives −0.005 ± 0.013 and D6 0.012 ± 0.020 mJy: too shallow to say anything.
  • What kept it open: an object seen at 3 µm and not at 1–2 µm is what the models of an infrared-bright Planet Nine describe, and 0.034 mJy is below the WISE limit. A noise peak in D4 looks exactly the same, so the four points above could not settle it.

The check in the WISE archive

WISE imaged every place twice a year at 3.4 µm, at the same 90° from the Sun as SPHEREx. A body of 0.034 mJy is far below one WISE exposure, but not below ten years of them added along its orbit (px/wise.py).

  1. Data. 856 NEOWISE exposures of 2014–2024 that overlap the strip the candidate crossed, 1.0° × 0.3°, as cutouts from IRSA: 21 epochs, 30–69 exposures each, 8–23 at any one place.
  2. Epoch images and differences. Every exposure goes on one sky grid in mJy; an epoch image is the median of its exposures; the static sky is the clipped mean of the other 20 epochs. Only static sources above about 0.1 mJy are masked, 16% of the strip.
  3. Flux scale. The static sky at 115 isolated CatWISE stars against their catalog fluxes; the scatter is 4%.
  4. The sum. The orbit is carried back to each epoch and the differences are added along it. Its uncertainty is scanned: distance 380–408 au, speed along the line of sight ±2 km/s, own motion ±0.04″/day, 2.3 million orbits. The same orbits shifted on the sky, 792 places, show what noise alone reaches.

  • What it gives the method. Any candidate at 3 µm can be tested this way at once, without waiting half a year for the next pass. Ten years of WISE reach half the noise of three SPHEREx passes in D4.

D4 alone is almost as deep as D1–D3 together. D5 and D6 are three to five times shallower than D4. The three-pass column is the per-pass errors combined, not a separate measurement.

What this means in magnitudes

  • The near-infrared flux at a given V depends on the surface. Red Sedna at V = 20.8 gives 0.037 mJy. Neutral Eris with methane ice at V = 18.7 gives 0.09 mJy: per unit of visible light, a third of Sedna's.
  • For a body of the color of Eris the blind limit is about V = 19 in one pass and V = 19.7 with three passes added; along a known track, about V = 19.7 in one pass.
  • For a body of the color of Sedna the blind limit is about V = 20 in one pass and V = 20.9 with three passes added; along a known track, about V = 21 in one pass and V = 21.5 in three.

Planet Nine

  • The predicted planet is V = 21 and fainter. The Pan-STARRS search has ruled it out down to V = 21.5 over most of the predicted region; with ZTF and DES that is 78% of the predicted cases. In reflected light a blind search in SPHEREx all-sky data stays short of that even with three passes added.
  • A chance remains only if the planet is much brighter in the infrared than in the visible. Fortney and co-authors (2016) show that a cold planet whose methane has frozen out can be far brighter at 3–5 µm than a blackbody. WISE searched for that at 3.4 µm down to W1 = 16.7, which is 0.065 mJy, and found nothing.
  • D4 covers the same wavelengths. Along a known track three passes of D4 reach 0.018 mJy, 3.6 times deeper than the WISE search. Blind, a search in D4 alone reaches 0.039 mJy in clean sky and 0.042–0.047 mJy near the ecliptic: 1.4–1.7 times deeper than WISE (the fourth step above). This is the one place where SPHEREx adds to the existing searches for Planet Nine, and the margin is small.
  • What SPHEREx does give for any candidate found elsewhere: a check of its place in three or more passes, its distance from the jump, and a 102-channel spectrum.

What is not tested yet

  • The test with artificial bodies covers the far range, 250–2000 au, in three fields; it was not made for the single-pass search or for the range of Sedna.
  • The far range has no real body to test on. It rests on the same code that found Eris and Sedna and on the artificial bodies.
  • The fields of the second and third passes of the test bodies were centred by the ephemeris. A real search reads a corridor along the line of places allowed by the distance; that step is not run yet.
  • The sum of passes for a body with no prior place at 30–150 au needs the outer passes over a strip of about 1°; not run. Makemake was not rerun with the second and third versions.
  • A search in D4 over the whole band where Planet Nine is predicted: two 1° fields were searched; the band is thousands of square degrees.
  • Code: motion_pipeline/px: px.py one pass, multi.py the sum of passes with the Planet Nine prior and the test with artificial bodies, check_multi.py, limit.py, follow.py a candidate in other detectors, wise.py a candidate in the WISE archive, link.py, link_faint.py, track.py; results in motion_pipeline/work_px.

sections.title: Bright bodies inside one visit: the search in the lab
sections.html:
What it does. When all the exposures of a field of 12′ or less have arrived (and the Gaia stars, which are needed to tell stars from movers), the lab searches them for moving objects by itself (about 0.2 to 4 s for 20 to 36 exposures). It marks unknown candidates (violet) and known small bodies (green) on every season and plays one visit in the film that opens from the line “inside a pass” of the row Movers of the Searches list. For a body that was opened by name it also stacks along its ephemeris. What it does not do: there is no survey of the archive; a single exposure reaches only about V 16 to 17; fields above 10′ are not searched by the lab yet (they have no old cube); the completeness of the blind search was measured only with synthetic movers added to the real candidates of one field (change log M13 and M15: it depends strongly on the rate, a faint fast mover is found in fewer than half of the trials at some rates), the stack’s completeness with artificial sources, and the false-track rate on a few fields (section 7). Candidates are candidates, not discoveries.

1. Detections in one exposure

  • Peaks: local maxima of the sky-subtracted image above 5σ (σ = the exposure's own noise from the service) with at least two neighbours above 1.5σ; peaks closer than 3 px are one source. A flagged neighbour does not disqualify a peak, and the pipeline's flag value 4 (the group TRANSIENT, PERSIST, OUTLIER, SNOWBALL, HALO, CROSSTALK, STREAK, GHOST, see the flag table; the core of a bright mover is often flagged OUTLIER) is not treated as bad for this search, for the Motion-only film or for the stack (since M12; before, the film and the stack dropped these pixels and the 3I/ATLAS stack peak was displaced by 5 px). The price: persistence, ghost and crosstalk pixels are kept too and can become false peaks. Not tested directly: the tracks are not checked in detector coordinates. The round-10 review argued that this is not a hole for artefacts fixed on the detector: the pointing steps by about 116 px (12′) every 2.2 minutes, so such an artefact would move about 75,000 px per day, far above the linker’s speed cap of 800 px per day, and persistence left by an earlier exposure is static on the sky. What remains is a chance line made of static clusters seen in one visit (no rule requires the detections to be spread along the line).
  • Saturated regions (flag bit 1): pixels within 2 px of each other form a region, which is ONE detection at its centre. No other detection is made within 4 px + 4 × the radius of the region (the halo of a saturated star is full of peaks that are not sources).
  • Matched filter for faint and slightly extended sources: the mean of 3 × 3 pixels in units of the independent-pixel noise; local maxima above 5.5 × the measured scatter of that filtered image ((84th − 16th percentile) / 2 of the exposure, never below 1, because neighbouring pixels are correlated). The threshold is raised until the negative image has at most one peak. In the eight checked fields (10 to 36 exposures each) the negative image keeps 3 to 24 peaks after the raise, 0.3 to 0.9 per exposure, against 534 to 2,079 positive peaks (most of them stars); before the raise it held 4 to 115. These residual false alarms are met again by the linking rules below; the false-track rate is measured below (section 7).

2. Stars are not movers

  • A Gaia star (G ≤ 17.5, moved to the SPHEREx epoch) within 0.9 px of a detection (3 px for a saturated region) removes it.
  • A position detected within 1.2 px in at least 3 exposures spread over at least min(3 days, 0.4 of the time covered by the loaded exposures) is a star. Detections more than 8 times brighter than the median of the faintest quarter of such a cluster (at least S/N 5) do not belong to it, so that a mover that passes over a faint static source is not taken for that source; saturated regions are never treated this way. A saturated region that sits at one place at two times at least 0.1 day apart is a star too (a body at 7 px/h would have moved).

3. Linking into tracks

In each visit (exposures less than half a day apart) every pair of detections in different exposures defines a straight line; detections within 1.0 px of it at their own time are collected (one per exposure). The line with the largest sum of min(S/N, 100) and at least 5 exposures wins, is refitted by least squares and removed, and the search repeats (up to 8 tracks per visit). A track is kept only if all of these hold:

  • its scatter is at most 0.7 px; its length is at least max(0.5 px, 2.4 px / √(median S/N / 5)) (three times the centroid error); its speed is between 0.5 and 800 px/day;
  • its detections are at least 45 % of the exposures whose footprint covers the predicted position while the track lasts;
  • inside every burst of three or more detections less than 6 minutes apart the detections move the way the line says (the shift across the burst may differ from the line's by 0.25 px + 2.5 × the burst's own scatter × √(12 / n) + 25 % of the expected shift);
  • it is proved by one of three things: a burst in which the expected shift is larger than that tolerance and was measured; detections in at least four separate epochs (gaps of more than 14 minutes); or a bright tight line (median S/N at least 50, scatter at most 0.6 px, at least 8 detections).

A weaker track of the same visit that runs within 10 px of a stronger one, at a speed within 50 % of it, is a companion (a piece of a saturated core or halo) and is dropped. The S/N shown for a track is the median of its detections.

4. Known bodies

IMCCE SkyBoT cones (geocentric) at the median epoch of each group of exposures (at most 0.5 day), each body moved linearly to the exposure time with the cone's rates and then to the spacecraft's viewpoint when the exposure carries the spacecraft position; bodies fainter than V 21 or with a position uncertainty above 120″ are left out. A body that the lab was opened on by name (sb=) is also taken from JPL Horizons as seen from the SPHEREx spacecraft (observer 500@-163182; numbered asteroids by their number; converted to pixels with the linear approximation (ΔRA·cos δ, ΔDec) of the tangent plane, accurate to about 0.2 px over 12′) at every exposure time; it replaces the SkyBoT entry of the same name and a track within 5 px of it is that body. If Horizons does not answer, the panel says so and only SkyBoT is used. SkyBoT's orbit of 3I/ATLAS is 12 to 16 px off, which is why Horizons is used for a named body. Unknown candidates are shown only after every known body has been asked for. A track is called a known body when the body lies within 2.5 px (5 px for a Horizons body) of it in at least half of its detections. Magnitudes are V for asteroids and Horizons' total magnitude (T) for comets.

5. On the seasons and in the film

On every season (Blink and Difference, not Co-add) the path during that season of each unknown track (violet, “candidate N”, the same number in the film and in the list) and of each known body brighter than V 18 or detected (green) is traced thinly, and the checkbox shows the count. The Movers button plays one visit: one frame per instant of exposure (the two exposures taken at the same moment share a frame), in time order. Every exposure is another wavelength, so a star would blink; therefore (1) each exposure is divided by its median brightness relative to the other exposures of the visit, measured on the static stars (peak of the 3 × 3 pixels, at least 5σ, not saturated, at least 3 stars; otherwise no scaling); (2) the static sky is the pixelwise median of the scaled exposures (at least 40 % of them valid). Field shows the scaled exposures. Motion only shows each scaled exposure minus the static sky, z = difference / √(σ² + (0.15 × static sky)²) (the 15 % is an ASSUMED allowance for the PSF changing with wavelength), each pixel's z limited to between −5 and 12 and the sum over 3 × 3 pixels divided by 3 (so a one-pixel spike cannot pass), drawn in amber from 5 to 17 over a dim copy of the static sky. A saturated pixel is drawn at full strength only if the static sky is faint there. Gaia stars (G ≤ 16.5: a disc of 2 px + 0.6 px per magnitude brighter than G 14), the stars found above (3 px, larger for saturated ones) and sources seen at one place at two times at least 0.02 day apart are masked; the place of a known body is never masked. The label “detected” is shown in the frames in which the track has a detection.

5b. Clicking a moving object, the candidate list and the investigation

On a field of up to 12′ the search runs by itself when the exposures have arrived, wherever the field is (a click on the globe, typed coordinates, a name). A click on a violet or a green trace (or on a row of “Moving objects in this field” on the Object tab) opens its card. Known body: name, class, expected magnitude and rate from IMCCE SkyBoT, its position in the exposure on show, whether the blind search found it, and, from the JPL Small-Body Database, the orbit, H and diameter when given. Candidate: rate and position angle, first and last detection (UT and sky position) from the fitted line, number of exposures, median S/N, scatter about the line, and a spectrum measured in a 2-pixel aperture that follows the line (the same aperture rules as for a fixed source, no aperture correction). Every unknown track is saved in a list kept in this browser (localStorage) once all known bodies have been asked for (when the service answered completely); the list is read again on every change, so two tabs share it; nothing is sent anywhere until you press Investigate, which sends the track’s positions and times to the sky service, which asks IMCCE SkyBoT and its Gaia cache; the same track found again (within 0.08 day and 25″ of the saved line) is not saved twice. The list is on the Findings page. Investigate asks IMCCE SkyBoT for every body within 120″ of the line at its first, middle and last epoch (no magnitude cut, geocentric; through the service endpoint /api/skybot_cone) and Gaia DR3 for sources within 12″ of the line's two ends. Bodies fainter than V 20 are ignored (a single exposure cannot see them; a magnitude of 0 means “not given”). It calls the track consistent with a known body when, at two of the three epochs, a body lies within the larger of 15″ plus 1.5 × 9.7″ / distance in au (the parallax of the spacecraft’s orbit, about 7,000 km from the Earth’s centre, against SkyBoT’s geocentric positions) and twice the orbit error SkyBoT gives, at a rate within 40 % and a position angle within 30° of the track’s; it calls it probably that body (a weaker verdict, status unchanged) when at all three epochs a body within 120″ has the rate within 10 % and the direction within 10° (comets have orbit errors of minutes of arc); otherwise it says that no known body matches and that the candidate still needs a second look. The matching does not use the candidate’s brightness beyond the V 20 cut, does not read the detector coordinates (see flag 4) and is not a substitute for the Minor Planet Center’s checker. The status, a note and a copyable report (position, UT, rate, DOIs) are kept with the candidate. A candidate is a lead, not a discovery: the false-track rate is not zero (section 3). Fields above 10′ are not searched yet. Parallax of the spacecraft: SPHEREx orbits at about 7,000 km from the Earth’s centre, so a body closer than about 1 au changes its position as seen from the spacecraft by up to 9.7″ / distance in au every 98 minutes (about 21″, 3.4 pixels, for a body at 0.46 au). What the linker does about it (since M15): the spacecraft’s geocentric position is known for every exposure (the sc_km of the exposure header); for each of the best seed lines the detections are also moved to the geocentre for six trial distances (0.08, 0.15, 0.3, 0.6, 1.2 and 2.5 au: observed minus geocentric = the spacecraft’s position projected on the sky / the distance), the line is fitted and gathered again in that frame, and the distance is adopted only if it gains at least two members or (with at least 8 members) lowers the scatter about the line by 30 %. The acceptance rules (scatter, burst consistency, number of epochs) then run in the geocentric frame; the stored detections and the drawn trace stay as observed, and the ring of the film adds the parallax back. A track that needed it is marked in the data (plxD). On 433 Eros (0.46 au) this turns a track that the burst-consistency rule rejected (scatter 0.53 px, inconsistent) into one that is accepted (0.36 px; distance 0.3 au fits best); with the opposite sign of the parallax it is not found, which is the check that the sign is right. The distance of the grid is a coarse stand-in for the real one and is not reported as a measurement. The film’s known positions are moved to the spacecraft’s viewpoint by the service, and so are the SkyBoT bodies of Investigate (the service’s /api/skybot_cone takes the exposure’s sc_km), so the 15″ tolerance there has no parallax allowance; a candidate saved before M15 has no spacecraft position and keeps the old allowance. The references are: IMCCE SkyBoT, Berthier et al. 2006 (ASP Conf. 351); JPL Horizons, Giorgini et al. 1996 (BAAS 28); JPL Small-Body Database (ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sbdb.cgi), the SBDB API.

6. Stack along the ephemeris of a named body

For every exposure that has the body in the field, the Motion-only z map (static sky subtracted, 3 × 3 matched; without the star masks, because the predicted position may lie next to a star) is read at the predicted position plus a trial offset (dx, dy) of up to 8 px, and the values are summed: T(dx, dy) = Σ z / √N, over offsets covered by at least 60 % of the exposures. The significance is empirical: the same search is made on 40 control paths (the ephemeris path moved by a fixed vector of 15 to 40 px, wrapped round the field so that coverage and stars are alike, so that at every exposure the body is at least 15 px away); the peak is a detection when it is higher than the peaks of all 40 control paths (p about 0.02). The panel gives the peak, its offset from the prediction and the number of control paths that beat it. Completeness: a fake point source (Gaussian, σ = 1 px, a given peak S/N per exposure) is added to the pixels of the exposures on a control path, at a random place 0.5 to 5 px from its centre, the z maps are recomputed, and it counts as recovered if the stack peak is higher than all the other control paths and within 1.5 px of the fake source; 20 trials per level, so every percentage is a multiple of 5 %. It tests the stack, not the blind search. Limits: on a saturated body the stack peaks several px from the prediction (the halo and the clipped core), so it is a detection test and not an astrometric one; the controls are noisy when the body sits in a bright halo or a crowded field; with the 6 px error of a prediction the offset search is wide enough, with a larger one it is not.

7. Checks

Eight known bodies (Vesta, Ceres, Pallas, Iris, Eugenia, Eros, 3I/ATLAS and the comet Lemmon) are checked on the Findings page with the numbers produced by Method M12 (each field loaded once; the search and the stack are deterministic: re-opening 45 Eugenia gave the same stack numbers to 15 digits); they are the only checks of the detections that exist. Completeness of the blind search by rate (synthetic movers added to the real candidates of the Eugenia field; scatter 0.2 + 2.5 / S/N px; detection probability 0.35 + 0.04 × S/N; 6 trials each; a body that crosses the middle of the field at a random time): at 27″/h peak S/N 8, 15, 30: 4, 6, 6 of 6; at 60″/h: 1, 3, 4 of 6; at 120″/h: 0, 1, 1 of 6. Fast bodies are in the field for a few hours and in few bursts, which the rules for a proved track do not accept; the search is therefore much less complete for fast movers than the S/N alone suggests (before M15 at 60 and 120″/h: 0 of 6). Known limits of the film: Motion only still shows some 7 to 20 amber spots per frame in the Eugenia field (1 to 11 at full strength, counted in the round-8 review): cosmic rays, hot pixels and stars whose shape differs between wavelengths; only the rings and the traces are claims, an amber spot without one is not. Pixels with flag value 4 are kept, so persistence ghosts can also show. A faint mover may be missed by the linker: with the model of the M13 change log the test recovers 5 of 6 at peak S/N 6 and 6 of 6 at 8 and above, but that is one geometry, one field and a model of the scatter and of the detection rate that are assumptions (real bursts, close pairs, crowded fields are not covered); the S/N levels of the artificial sources of the stack are peak-pixel values, about 3.5 times below a matched-filter S/N. False tracks: the times of the exposures are shuffled inside each visit (positions and brightness of the detections kept, so that no real mover lines up) and the whole linker, with all the acceptance rules, is run again: 0 tracks in 16 shuffles for 45 Eugenia (34 exposures, 487 candidate detections), 0 in 10 for 7 Iris (36 exposures), 1 track in 16 for C/2025 A6 (10 exposures, 95 candidates, a crowded field); these counts are from Methods M7–M9. After the linker change of M12 and the burst correction of M13: 0 in 8 for 45 Eugenia (and 0 in 6 for C/2025 A6 with M12; an independent run of the round-9 review found 0 in 316 for that field and 2 in 15 for a field the rules were not tuned on, with 29 visits). The mean is below 0.1 false track per visit, with an upper limit of about 0.2 to 0.3 per visit at 95 %; it was measured on three fields only, and the rules were tuned on these same fields. The real movers' own detections are among the candidates and are shuffled too, which makes the count slightly pessimistic for chance alignments; but the shuffle cannot show false tracks made by correlated artefacts (ghosts, persistence), so the false-track rate it gives is a lower bound. The filter, the thresholds and the acceptance rules were tuned while looking at these same fields, so they are not an independent test.

sections.title: Spectral anomaly map
sections.html:
The spectrum of every source in the field is compared with an ordinary star of the same field. Only those that do not look like it are marked.

What you see and why

Motion is not the only sign of an interesting object. Every source in the field has a spectrum of hundreds of points, one per exposure. Almost all sources are ordinary stars, and their spectra look alike. The map puts a ring on those that do not, and on click shows exactly how they differ: the white dots are the source spectrum, the blue line is the ordinary star closest to it.

Barnard's Star field, 20′: 352 sources, 344 have a usable spectrum, 11 are above the threshold. The catalogs were opened only after the test. For four of the five most unusual sources Gaia gives a parallax of 5–8 mas and a BP−RP color from 2.6 to 3.0: these are red dwarfs 130–190 parsecs from us. The ordinary sources of the field are distant giants with a parallax of 0.1–1.5 mas and a color of 0.9–1.5. The dwarf spectra deviate from the giants by 13–19%: their peak near 1.6 µm is lower, the long-wavelength part is higher.

The most unusual source is too faint for Gaia (G = 21.3, no parallax); it is not identified. Barnard's Star itself and six more bright stars are saturated and are not in the map.

A map layer for coordinate mode: it shows the unusual without any motion at all.

How it is computed

# 1. source list: search between passes, 12σ threshold; for tracks, the position at the frame date
# 2. spectrum of each: the file is opened once, all sources are measured by PSF fitting (as in Spectrum on click)
for exp in exposures:
    for s in sources: s.pts.append(psf_flux(exp, s.position(exp.mjd)))      # (wavelength, flux, error)
# 3. 24 bins in ln λ from 0.75 to 5.0 µm: median and error in each
f[s, b], e[s, b] = median, 1.25 * MAD / sqrt(n)
shape[s] = f[s] / sum(f[s])
# 4. family of ordinary stars: median shape + 2 principal components of the bulk of the sources
med = median(shape[bright half]);  pc1, pc2 = svd(shape[bulk] - med)[:2]
# 5. anomaly: residual after fitting the family, in units of the error
model = a * (med + c1 * pc1 + c2 * pc2)                                     # a, c1, c2 are fitted
score[s] = sqrt(mean(((shape[s] - model) / sqrt(e**2 + (0.05 * model)**2))**2))
anomalous = score > median(score) + 6 * 1.4826 * MAD(score)
  • Two components are needed so that temperature and reddening are not counted as an anomaly: they shift a star's spectrum smoothly, and the family describes that.
  • The family is built from the field itself, without a library of spectra. The downside: in a field where most sources are unusual, the ordinary ones will come out as unusual.
  • An error floor of 5% of the model keeps bright stars with tiny errors from landing among the anomalies because of systematics.
  • A source on a track is measured along it. Otherwise its spectrum is truncated, and it lands among the anomalies for a false reason.
  • Time: 352 sources in 359 exposures take about two minutes on one core.
  • The map does not say what the object is. It says “not like the rest”; after that come the catalogs and a look at the spectrum by eye.
  • Code: fieldspec.py, anomaly.py, vids_j.py.

Second example: ε Indi B

20′ field: 103 sources, 102 spectra, 11 above the threshold. First by a huge margin is ε Indi B itself: its spectrum deviates by 167%, which is 92 times farther than the scatter of the field. The map found it without using motion. Next come seven faint red sources: in Gaia they have G from 19 to 21, and for six the parallax is not measured or not significant; in WISE the W1−W2 color is from 0.15 to 0.43, and three are flagged as extended. Most likely these are galaxies; no spectra from the literature were compared. One more source is a nearby red dwarf with a parallax of 22.8 mas.

sections.title: Thermal signature
sections.html:
One number that says whether a moving object only reflects sunlight or also shines by its own heat.

What you see and why

When something moves, the next question is what it is: a rock that reflects sunlight, or a body warm enough to glow by itself, such as a warm asteroid or a brown dwarf. Two measurements of the same object answer it: its brightness at 3.8–4.4 µm divided by its brightness at 1.1–1.6 µm. Sunlight is much fainter at 4 µm than at 1.3 µm, so a gray surface that only reflects it has a ratio of 0.23 (computed for the Sun, 5772 K), and so do ordinary stars. A larger ratio means light at 4 µm that the Sun did not supply: the heat of the object itself.

In the picture the path of each moving object is colored by this number: white at 0.23, red above it, blue below it. The gray dots on the scale are the stars of the field; they show where “nothing special” lies.

For the 345 stars of the Barnard's Star field the median of this ratio is 0.23; for the 101 stars of the ε Indi field it is also 0.23. The moving objects:

Object1.1–1.6 µm3.8–4.4 µmRatio
(4008) Corbin0.36 mJy0.14 mJy0.39 ± 0.06
(15101) 2000 AY1500.26 mJy0.48 mJy1.85 ± 0.30
ε Indi B22.2 mJy46.3 mJy2.08 ± 0.13

Corbin is close to pure reflection. 2000 AY150 has twice as much at 4 µm as at 1.3 µm: this is what the heat of the asteroid itself should look like. ε Indi B shines on its own. Barnard's Star and ε Indi A are saturated; there is no ratio for them, and the path stays gray.

In the application it is one line in the card of a moving object: the ratio with its error and what it means in words (reflects sunlight, or shines by its own heat). The colored path is how the video shows the same number.

How it is computed

# object spectrum along the track: rows (wavelength, flux, error)
def band(pts, lo, hi):
    v = pts.flux[(pts.lam >= lo) & (pts.lam < hi)]
    return mean(v), max(std(v), median(err)) / sqrt(len(v))
a, ea = band(pts, 1.10, 1.63)            # detector D2
b, eb = band(pts, 3.82, 4.42)            # detector D5
ratio = b / a;   err = ratio * hypot(ea / a, eb / b)
sun = mean(B_nu(3.82..4.42, 5772 K)) / mean(B_nu(1.10..1.63, 5772 K))      # 0.229
t = log(ratio / sun) / log(5 / sun)      # −1..1
colour = white → red for t > 0,  white → blue for t < 0
  • The bands follow detectors D2 and D5 for a reason: SPHEREx exposes with both at the same time. An asteroid rotates and changes brightness, but both numbers refer to the same minutes.
  • The asteroid fluxes come from the measurement along the ephemeris with the light of the stars under the object subtracted (check on asteroids). The ε Indi B fluxes come from the spectra of all sources in the field (the anomaly map).
  • One number does not separate the causes. The ratio grows with heat, with a red slope of the reflectance, and with emission of the object's own. It sorts objects; it does not identify them.
  • Code: thermal.py, vids_k.py.

Second example: ε Indi B

In the ε Indi field the blind search found two tracks. ε Indi B has a ratio of 2.08 ± 0.13: nine times larger than for the field stars. ε Indi A is saturated, its path is gray. There were no known asteroids brighter than V = 19.5 in the cutouts of this field: JPL answered for 41 of the 60 days of observations; the remaining queries did not get a response.

sections.title: Globe, coverage and catalogs
sections.html:
• Sky background: five choices with plain names. Dust map is the all-sky infrared dust map (SFD), real survey data stored as one image. Optical — DSS2, Near-infrared — 2MASS and Infrared — WISE (AllWISE bands W1, W2 and W4 as blue, green and red) are all-sky surveys from the HiPS mirror of IRSA: the service fetches each tile once and keeps it. The Allsky image of tile order 3 (64 × 64 pixels per tile, about 0.11° per pixel) fills the whole sky; zooming in, the tiles of the order that fits the scale (512 pixels per tile, down to about 0.4″ for DSS2) are read and the Allsky image shows until they arrive. The backgrounds are context only; the exposure coverage layer stays on top.
  • Exposure coverage: the service's HEALPix map (NESTED, order 3, 768 cells of about 7.3° on a side). A cell is coloured if at least one exposure footprint touches it; teal = QR2 present, blue = QR3 only; brightness = log(1 + number of exposures) relative to the busiest cell. The cell shapes are exact HEALPix corners, projected for the globe or the Mollweide map. Until the exposure index is complete the layer shows only the indexed periods (the Archive page states how many).
  • Exposure count at the aim: the service's coverage preview for the chosen field; shown only once the index is complete, because a partial index would give a wrong count.
  • Search: names and coordinates. Names not in the local snapshot go to SIMBAD live (through the service); the snapshot is a fixed list of 3,810 stars, brown dwarfs and variables queried from SIMBAD earlier (its kinds are SIMBAD object types mapped to plain words).
  • Small bodies: the JPL Small-Body Database query API, 25 per page (about 1.58 million asteroids, 4,087 comets at the time of writing): H, diameter, albedo, a, e, i exactly as JPL gives them. “Position today” is the geocentric position from JPL Horizons for the current time (V magnitude from the H, G model). Open in lab loads the exposures of the passage, and the moving-object search of the lab follows the body through them (see section “Moving objects”).

Ready-made toolsall stepsastropy is the base; what else was considered is listed below

Service

  • The sky service (service/: Python, astropy, numpy, scipy) finds the exposures of a field in its own index of the whole archive and reads only the image rows it needs from the public S3 copy; what it has read is cached by file.
  • The super-frames are computed once per field: one stack per pass and detector as 16-bit floats, with the pass dates, the wavelength and flux of each exposure, the target centroids and the saturated share. For a 5′ field on the 1.54″ grid that is 18 images of 208 × 208, under 2 MB whatever the number of exposures; the cutouts behind them are 1.8 GB, so the cache is mandatory.
  • The portrait and the searches need the single exposures and are computed on request.

Browser

  • The pendulum, the spectral color and the wall are computed from the same stacks, so switching between them needs no new data: in WebGL2 they are fragment shaders over the stacks held as R16F textures.
  • The lab is being moved onto this scheme. Today the service still sends it every exposure and the browser combines them itself (status table in section 1).

What “spectra on the fly” means

Level 2 data contain no ready-made spectrum of an object. Each exposure sees the object at one wavelength, different for each position on the detector. The spectrum has to be assembled: the object is measured in every exposure and the flux is plotted against wavelength.

“On the fly” means: on a click, for any point of the sky, from the same exposures that are already read for the picture, with no ready-made catalog. A moving object adds a subtlety: it has to be measured where it was at the time of each exposure, that is, along its track. A service for fixed coordinates cannot do this.

Why the search needs it: the spectrum says what exactly is moving. A cold dwarf or a planet has methane and water bands and a rise toward 4–5 µm. An asteroid shows reflected sunlight plus a thermal rise beyond 3.5 µm. A star declines smoothly.

How far it is tested: on an ordinary star (347 points from 358 exposures, within 2–3% of 2MASS and WISE), on a cold dwarf (ε Indi B, 414 points) and on moving objects (two 18th-magnitude asteroids along their ephemerides, with a control next to the track that gives zero). For the saturated Barnard's Star only a rough draft is possible. Not tested: objects with no known orbit.

Ready-made tools: what is used and what is not

  • astropy is the base: FITS reading, pixel coordinates and the wavelength of every pixel through astropy.wcs, the position of the Earth for the orbit model.
  • numpy and scipy: stacking, filters, fits.
  • Catalogs and ephemerides are asked from the services themselves over HTTP (IRSA TAP and cutouts, SIMBAD, Gaia, JPL Small-Body Identification and Horizons, IMCCE SkyBoT). astroquery wraps the same requests and is not needed.
  • photutils offers source detection and PSF photometry. Our PSF fit is about a hundred lines (spec.py) because it has to read both PSF formats of the releases and to keep the pixels flagged OUTLIER when a moving object is measured.
  • reproject brings frames onto a common grid. We keep our own stacking: it preserves fine detail when the pixel is as large as the star.
  • astroscrappy (L.A.Cosmic) was tested for cosmic-ray hits and rejected: with a pixel this large it cannot tell a star from a hit (step 5).
  • Aladin Lite would show other surveys under our pictures with no code of ours. It is not used: the CDS servers it loads from did not respond from our network. What it does not do in any case is stack SPHEREx exposures, blink the passes and search for motion.

sections.title: What worked on the data and where to be careful
sections.html:
Proper motion of Barnard's Star from three SPHEREx passes: 10.40″/yr, direction 353°. Gaia DR3 catalog: 10.39″/yr, 356°. The residual error of aligning the passes on field stars is 0.05″.
  • Barnard's Star is too bright for SPHEREx: the core is saturated in every frame. These pixels hold no measurements: they are white in every picture and nothing is painted in.
  • The spectrum in the portrait is crudely calibrated. The flux at 1.25 µm came out at about 12 Jy against 12.8 Jy from 2MASS, but steps of ×0.6–0.7 remain at the detector boundaries, and the scatter of the points in D2–D3 reaches 20–25%. The water dips are only hinted at. On an unsaturated star the problem did not recur: there the scatter is 1–4% and the boundaries have no steps.
  • A calibrated spectrum of Barnard's Star cannot be obtained from these files. We tried three methods, each checked against 2MASS on bright field stars:
    • PSF fit to the wings. The PSF tables in the files are cut off at about 2.5–3 pixels: at 3–3.5 pixels real stars are 3–4 times brighter than the table, farther out — tens of times. On eight bright stars the result was from 0.68 to 1.54 of the catalog value.
    • Flagged pixels near the core. With the overflow flag the values are too low: by 0–3% for a star with J = 8.6 and by 4–13% for J = 7.4. With the transient and processing-failure flags they are, on the contrary, too high: by 8–24% for J = 8.6 and by 21–36% for J = 7.4–7.7.
    • The unflagged halo at 3.5–7 pixels against a profile taken from seven stars with J = 8.5–9.4. On independent stars with J = 7.1–8.1 the result was 0.70–1.16 of the catalog value. For Barnard's Star — 1.10 in J, 1.69 in H and 1.81 in Ks: its halo per unit of catalog flux is one and a half to two times brighter than that of stars two to four magnitudes fainter.
    Conclusion: for a star with a saturated core, Level 2 data support the shape of the spectrum within one detector (in D4–D6 the scatter is 2–4%), but not its level and not the steps between detectors.
  • The spectrum on click was tested on stars of one field (ten bright, five faint) and on two asteroids. The W2 band extends beyond the SPHEREx range and was left out of the comparison. It has not been tested on cold dwarfs or on objects with no known orbit.
  • The blind search for objects that cross the field in days linked tracks in a field near the ecliptic: four, and all four are known asteroids with V = 18.1–18.8. Three were linked from 5–7 visits. The fourth was linked from three visits and confirmed by flux in four more. Fainter than V = 19 it links no tracks. A triple of visits proves nothing by itself: the control gives 3.5 random triples per trial, and only triples confirmed by flux at the positions along the orbit are accepted. The distance from the curvature of the path agreed with JPL within 4–13% for four asteroids at 2–3 au; at other distances this has not been tested. Of 94 verified sources, 69 are unidentified and look like noise near the threshold. In the dense field of Barnard's Star the same search linked no tracks: the two known asteroids there give one verified visit between them.
  • The OUTLIER flag in Level 2 files is set on asteroid pixels in 72% of exposures. Such pixels do not go into the super-frames, and that is right for the fixed sky; in a search for moving objects they have to be kept.
  • For ε Indi B three passes out of four are used: the pipeline code is written for three passes (the lab takes any number). The passes are aligned on only five stars. Of 140 sources in the 20′ field, the search failed to match three between passes.
  • For ε Indi B, in some of the D5 and D6 visits a faint streak (0.1–0.2 MJy/sr) runs from the object. Comparing visits rejects it, but the cause is not established, and its far end in D6 remains in the video. Wide stacks are not cleaned by this check.
  • The spectrum of ε Indi B deviates from the catalogs more than the spectra of ordinary stars: by 7–9% in J and H and by 20% in W1. The cause is not established.
  • In the 60′ field the shift of the star, estimated with a crude centroid on the wide stack, came out at 9.4″, in the 20′ field — 9.9″, against 10.2″ from the narrow frames. A discrepancy of up to 0.9″ is one seventh of a SPHEREx pixel; wide stacks are good for display, not for astrometry.
  • The parallax is caught but not measured: the March point deviates by 1.7″ against an expected 1.0″.
  • In D1 exposures a band of +1.4 MJy/sr runs across the frame at a wavelength of 1.07–1.09 µm. By wavelength this is the 1.083 µm helium line in the glow of the upper atmosphere; the zodiacal background model does not remove it. In wide stacks it is subtracted as a wavelength-dependent background.
  • One exposure out of 359 is discarded: the target fell on the edge of the detector.
  • Of the five test targets of the challenge statement, two went through the whole pipeline: Barnard's Star and ε Indi B. The archive holds 256 exposures of WISE 0855, 333 of RW Aurigae and 2483 of R Draconis (near the ecliptic pole, in the deep field); all five open in the lab.

The sky service and the lab

The service is the research project's reference implementation; its validation (wavelength calibration against IRSA, parallax, depth, comparisons with SPIFF and JWST spectra for ε Indi B and WISE 0855, AAVSO photometry for RW Aur and R Dra) is documented in the project's analysis files. What is checked in this application: counts of exposures per band and season are printed for every field; the cube cap (1,500 exposures) are stated; the single-frame 5σ depth is 18.3 / 18.3 / 18.4 / 18.2 / 17.4 / 16.9 AB for D1–D6 (PSF fit, ±0.4 mag; an aperture of 2 px reaches about 1 mag less).

Known limits: pixel values are shipped by the service as 16-bit floats, whose rounding (about 0.1 % of the value) approaches the noise only in the halo of very bright stars; when an exposure's σ is missing the value 0.05 MJy/sr is used; the service's own photometry endpoints use a 6–9 px sigma-clipped annulus while this application's point spectra use a 4–8 px unclipped median, so their numbers differ slightly; the RA/Dec boxes of the Controls show the catalogue (J2000) position while the Object card shows the position moved to the observation epoch; no PSF matching; sky subtraction is the exposure median; no deblending of close pairs; the cube holds at most 1,500 exposures (R Dra has about 2,485); 6.15″ pixels blur small features when a 3′ field is shown large.

Bands between passes. Exposures of different passes sample different wavelengths inside the same band. A change of a band image between passes can therefore reflect another part of the spectrum, not a change of the source; a change is claimed only at matched wavelengths (section “Object card”).
